speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. Sir ROBERT BORDEN (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: VOTE OF THANKS TO THE LORD MAYOR AND .SHERIFFS OF LONDON.
speechtext:
I beg to move, seconded by Sir Wilfrid Laurier:
That this House do accept the Mace presented in 1916 by Colonel the Rt. Hon Sir Charles Cheers Wakefield, then Lord Mayor of London, and by Sir George Alexander Touche, M.P., and Sir Samuel George Shead, then Sheriffs of London, and that the warm thanks of the House be conveyed by Mr. Speaker to the donors.
The House will remember that shortly after the fire which destroyed the Parliament Buildings we were in receipt of a communication from the then Lord Mayor and the Sheriffs of London in which they asked to be permitted to present a mace to this House to take the place of that which unfortunately had been destroyed in the fire. I consulted with my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) at that time, and we agreed that the offer should be accepted. The mace has been prepared by the Goldsmiths and Silversmiths Company, Ltd., and during my recent visit to England it was presented to me in order that I might transmit it to Mr. Speaker and obtain the formal assent of the House to its acceptance. The mace is now on the Table, and McC.ea.]
hon. gentlemen have had an opportunity of examining it. I am sure they will all agree that it is a very beautiful piece of workmanship, and that the warm thanks of the House are due to Sir Charles Wakefield, Sir George Touche, and Sir Samuel Shead for their generous gift. This gift and its acceptance form a new link of association between the Parliament of Canada and the great city at the heart of our Empire.
I might perhaps with advantage place on Hansard a description of the design of the mace, which has been prepared by the Goldsmiths and Silversmiths Company:
The general design of the Mace is on similar lines to that used in the English House of Commons. The vase shaped head is divided into four panels by female figures with acanthus leaf terminals. These panels contain the following beautifully embossed emblems. The Arms of the Dominion of Canada, the Rose for England, the Harp for Ireland, and the Thistle for Scotland; above each emblem 'is the Royal Crown and the initials G. OR. are placed on either side. In the spaces above the figures is shown the Beaver executed in bold relief. The Head of the Mace is supported by four ornamental brackets and is surmounted by the Royal Crown, indicating the Royal Authority; beneath the arches where the cushion is usually placed, there is a raised circular space on which appears in relief the full blazon of the Royal Arms of Great Britain and Ireland. The Staff is divided at intervals by two spiral fluted knops, and the whole length is richly chased with the Rose, Shamrock, Thistle and the Maple Leaf. The massive foot of the Staff is decorated with Roses, Thistles and Fleur-de-lys, the plain space above bearing the following inscription:-
'This Mace replacing the original Mace of the House of Commons of the Dominion of Canada, destroyed by fire on February 17th, 1916, was presented by Colonel the Rt. Hon. Sir Charles Cheers Wakefield, Lord Mayor of London, and the Sheriffs of London, George Alexander Touche, Esq., M.P., and Samuel George Shead, Esq., June, 1916.'
In its design and execution the Mace forms an emblem of authority well worthy of the great country for which it is intended.
It will be observed that the date of the destruction of the Parliament Buildings is incorrectly stated in the inscription. I am at a loss to know how this mistake could have occurred, but I have no doubt it can be easily rectified. The Lord Mayor of London placed the Council Chamber of the Guild Hall at the disposal of the donors for the purpose of presenting the mace, and he himself attended and presided over the ceremony. Each of the donors spoke and their expressions of goodwill to this country and of appreciation of the part which Canada is taking in the great struggle in which we are now engaged were all that any of us could desire. I am sure there will be a perfect unanimity of feeling in

the House in assenting to this resolution, and I trust that Mr. Speaker will convey in fitting terms to the donors the appreciation and thanks of the House, together with a copy of the resolution which I am now proposing.
Right hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER: On Friday, we shall know exactly what my right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) has brought back from his visit to England. Yet even to-day we see and must acknowledge that he has not come back empty-handed, but on the contrary he has brought in this mace a very substantial evidence of the work he has accomplished on the other side of the water. This emblem and its presentation are evidences of our connection and growing relations with the Motherland. For my part, though I am a democrat to the hilt, I certainly appreciate all these evidences of our parliamentary history as it has come down to us through the ages. All these symbols and ceremonies have their uses. I-t may be that when a new member comes to this House, he may think it somewhat archaic when he sees the sergeant-at-arms with the mace preceding the Speaker, but when he becomes better acquainted with Parliament, he finds that each of these customs has its significance. One of England's historic personages called the mace a "bauble," and ordered it out of the Commons, but its restoration signified the restoration to England of constitutional government as it exists to-day. Parliamentary government has come from England to Canada, and this gift to us is an emblem of those parliamentary institutions which are so highly prized, especially now that we are under fire in the present world war.
Motion agreed to.

subsubtopic: GRAND TRUNK PACIFIC AND TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAYS.
speechtext: 1 and 2. The reasons for the Government's action, in. this matter are set out in a letter from the Chairman of the Ra'lway Commission, as follows:

subtopic: BOARD OF RAILWAY COMMISSIONERS FOR CANADA.

speechtext:
Ottawa, May 7th, 1917.
Dear Sir:-
I have your letter of to-day's date raising the question as to why the rails of the Canadian Northern through the Yellowhead Pass be not taken up in place of the rails of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

While I admit that the Canadian Northern construction through the Yellowhead Pass is of a high order and with low grades, nevertheless, they have a sub-summit on their track. This the Grand Trunk Pacific has not. The Grand Trunk Pacific, of course, are subject to a considerable operating expense in removing sand from their tracks which regularly blows over them when the water in the river is low. The Canadian Northern is not subject to this disability, which, according to the Grand Trunk Pacific, entails an extra cost of some $25,006 a year for maintenance.
Bearing in mind, not only the character of the Canadian Northern track, but also the disability the Grand Trunk Pacific suffers from, owing to the sand, in my view there is no doubt but that the Grand Trunk Pacific is the better line of the two.
I have gone carefully into the matter of train resistance and economies of operation; and there is no doubt that, on the economic ground, the Canadian Northern rails should be lifted instead of the Grand Trunk Pacific. The difficulty is that I am unable to make any recommendation from a purely economic standpoint. Indeed, from this standpoint, no rails whatever ought to be lifted and transferred to France from the Yellowhead. The long railway haul itself and the use of railway equipment would forbid any such action on economic grounds. Further, this country is itself in need of rails, and when unnecessary duplications are removed, they can be usefully used in the Prairie sections which are to-day in need of railway construction.
The difficulty is that the question cannot be so approached. Canada, having acceded to the request of the Imperial Government to supply rails urgently required for military purposes in France, it became the duty of the country to supply these rails with as little cost as possible to the Imperial Government. This, of course, meant lifting rails in eastern territory, so as to reduce the cost of the railway haul, and also lifting rails where the least damage would be occasioned, not only to the public, but also to the companies owning and operating them, not only in the interests of the companies, but also in the interests of the Imperial Government, who would be expected to recompense the companies, not only for their rails, but also for the damages which the companies suffered.
The first request of the Imperial Government was finally confined to 300 miles of track. This amount the management of the Government railways were able to furnish, and at the same time carry on the business of the line. The rails of the Government lines fulfilled the requirements of the Imperial Government; they were in eastern territory; and, speaking generally, did not necessitate a long penalizing rail haul. The rails could also be lifted without creating liability for damages.
The Imperial Government required rails of a high class. Fortunately the rails of the Transcontinental answered in every respect. The Imperial authorities also required absolute standardization, owing to the fact that the laying of the rails in France would, in many instances, require the greatest despatch, and be laid under conditions of danger and often at night.
Their request for an additional 300 miles of track, to which request, as I understand it, the Government has acceded, requires that the
additional supply of rail should be similar in all respects to the rail already supplied.
While the rail of the Canadian Northern through the Yellowhead is of the required type and weight, unfortunately the engineers of the different lines in their specifications have for reason^ best known to themselves, bored the rails used by their respective companies at different points. This requires, of course, different angle-bars, and does not permit the different lengths being interchangeable, as I am informed for military reasons is necessary.
As personally I would somewhat sooner lift the Canadian Northern than the Grand Trunk Pacific rails, the question of re-boring, practically slotting, the Canadian Northern rails has been looked into. I am advised that this is impracticable, owing to the weakening of the rail. The matter was looked into by one of the engineers of your department, and Major Bell so reports; and Mr. Fitzgerald, of the Imperial Munitions Board, with whom I took this matter up, gives me the same advice.
Under the circumstances, I can only advise the removal of the Grand Trunk Pacific rails, interchangeable as they are with the rails already supplied by the National Transcontinental.
In my view, the proper final solution in the Yellowhead is, however, the retention of the Grand Trunk Pacific right-of-way rather than the Canadian Northern, and that the rails of the Canadian Northern, if these companies are in future to run in joint operation, should be placed on the Grand Trunk Pacific right-of-way.
The Grand Trunk Pacific rails ought to be lifted with care, so as to not injure the roadbed, and the sleepers should be left as they are at present embedded in it, so that other rails, may be there again laid with a maximum of expense. Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) H. L. Drayton,
Chief Commissioner. The Honourable the Minister of Railways and Canals, Ottawa, Ont.

That, in the opinion of this House, the question of extending the franchise to women should engage the attention of the Government at the present session.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in speaking on the motion now before the House, I desire to state that I have been very largely actuated by a consciousness of the need of a uniform Dominion Franchise Act for the whole of Canada. For many years past, the voters' lists of the various provinces have been used as the lists upon which the members of the House of Commons have been, elected and they are so used at the present time. That a gradual evolution has taken place since the adoption of these lists is quite evident when you consider the uniformity that existed when the present Act was adopted about twenty years ago and contrast it with the wide disparity which now exists between the franchises of the various provinces. The troublous and trying times through which we are passing have doubtless had a good deal to do with the rapid change that has taken place in the sentiment of the people during the past few years. The present is, I may say, a testing time when the essential qualifications entitling a person to the full status of citizenship become apparent.
The motion before the House refers only to the extension of the franchise to the women of Canada. That this would be a somewhat radical istep I am free to admit but we are living in an age when radical changes are taking place on every hand, when old traditions and conventions are being brushed aside, when despotism and democracy are being tested and tried, and



when we are called upon to exert every energy in the critical struggle in which we are now engaged. It is significant that the newer provinces of western Canada peopled with a young and virile population have blazed the way in the matter of extending the franchise (to the women. In the province of British Columbia woman suffrage is now an assured fact. In the great provinces of Alberta, (Saskatchewan and Manitoba the franchise has been extended to women. The legislature of the older province of Ontario at its last session adopted similar legislation. Today, from the Capital where we are at present assembled westward to the Pacific, the women of all the provinces exercise the full legal status of citizenship. Yet, from the Capital eastward to the Atlantic, that privilege or right has not as yet been conferred upon them. While it is undoubtedly the prerogative of the provinces to enact legislation regulating their municipal and provincial franchises, I feel it to be the duty of this House and of the Government to see that a uniform Franchise Act is adopted for the whole of Canada.
The whole of the people of Canada go to make up the state. The need of the state and the duties of citizenship weie never more clear or well defined than at this hour. I would also embody such provision in the Elections Act as would safeguard the rights of the state and prevent any one who is not -a loyal British subject from exercising the right to say how the affairs of this lD|ominion should 'be conducted. When you think of the people who have come from many of the European countries and settled in our midst, when you realize tl e cosmopolitan character of the population of Canada, some regulation, some safeguard, is necessary at this particular time with regard to the exercise of the rights of citizenship. I would also provide that no loyal British subjects should be debarred from the right of polling their votes in Canada and that is exactly what I have in mind in the introduction of this resolution.
While it may be true, and it undoubtedly is true, that many women do not desire to have the franchise extended to them, we cannot close our eyes to the fact that many women in Canada do desire to have this right conferred upon them. When you reflect that half the people of this Dominion arrogate to themselves the status of citizenship and deny that right to the other half, physically weaker but intellectually their equal, you cannot close your eyes to the fact that Prussian despotism 
is not confined to Germany alone. Freedom and liberty are the watchwords of the hour. Deny to our women the right to- be a participating factor in the affairs of our country and you are in duty bound to see that they have become wards of the state. The Indians of Canada have become wards of the state and have been disfranchised and an Indian Department has been established with the view of providing for their wants and requirements. The Indian is, in the eyes of the law, an infant, yet the Indian, by severing h!s tribal allegiance, can obtain the status of citizenship.
Our women are not wards of the State, nor yet are they the recipients of any favours or consideration that should bar them from receiving the rights which men have appropriated to themselves. It is true that Indians, women and children are the only classes in Canada who have not had conferred upon them the full legal status of citizenship. The Indian, by renouncing his tribal allegiance, can come into that state. The child, if a male, through the passing of time will eventually reach that condition where he becomes a full-fledged citizen of this country with a legal right to a voice in the affairs of state. It is only the women of Canada who are barred from reaching that condition. You cannot close your eyes to the heroic selfdenial, the devoted services, that have been rendered by the women of this country to maintain our laws, and to uphold the traditions of our country, and the devoted services which they have rendered since the beginning of this war. While I say since the beginning of this war, the women of Canada have, since the earliest days of our history, devoted themselves to making Canada the country which it is to-day. I believe, though, that during the past few years the heroic services which have been rendered by them have broken down the prejudice which formerly existed against extending the franchise to them. I believe that their part in this war has established in the minds of every one a belief in -their right to be a participating factor in the affairs of our country. It is surely a sad commentary on our discretion and judgment that we extend to the ignorant and illiterate foreigner, centuries behind us in moral and intellectual development, who comes to our country, concessions that are not given to all the people of Canada, and allow him to establish himself in any community, and, by a short residence among us and compliance with what is to him a very simple condition, give him the full

legal status of citizenship. And yet, in the face of that, we deny to these loyal, patriotic, God-fearing women of Canada equal consideration, when we deny them the consideration that has been given to those people who come here, who very often are not in sympathy with our laws or the traditions of our country. I say that it is a sorry reflection upon the people of this country that such a condition as that can exist, particularly at this time.
I could cite the examples of other countries in which the franchise has been extended to women, but I will not do so; I am going to confine my few remarks this afternoon to our own country. We know the conditions of our own country, and if we want a precedent, there is to my mind one country to which we are justified in looking for a precedent, that is the Mother Country. We find that the women of Great Britain have been promised the franchise by the Government of that country. The full extent of the franchise which is granted to them I do not as yet know; but we may rest assured that when Britain, the mother of parliaments, the champion of freedom and liberty, the champion of the weak, takes the part she is taking in granting to the women of that country the franchise, this is surely a precedent that we can well follow in the Dominion of Canada. I have already stated that the time of trial and stress through which we are passing has possibly made more clear to our minds the injustice which has been, done to the women of this country by withholding from them the franchise. I would not for a moment argue that any special treatment should be given to them. But I do say that we must endeavour to see that a truly national spirit is cultivated and developed among the people of this country, and that the conditions under which we are living at the present time -make it necessary for us to enact legislation whi-ch under ordinary conditions we would hesitate to enact. There are 'people living here within the borders of Canada but who have not yet become truly Canadianiized. Natives of countries with whom we and our Allies are to-day contending are granted- the franchise, and I believe some provision should be embodied in the Dominion Franchise Act to see that these people shall not have the opportunity of injuring or destroying in any way the work that is being done by the men who are waging battle for us at the front. I want to say further that when you think of the costly 94 i
and immortal sacrifice that is being daily offered up on the .altar of freedom, -we must realize that we are called upon to look on these matters from a new viewpoint. We must realize that it is the duty of Parliament and of the Government to deal with these questions with a firm and strong hand. We must also realize that there are many homes in Canada whose bread winners have -already given up their life blood for the cause of freedom, and that many more will do so. That being the ease, there are and there will be many widows and female relations of those men here in Canada who will become responsible for the families of these men, it is just and right that these women should be enabled to exercise the franchise? Yet, under present conditions, they are barred from doing so. I say that justice, humanity and the best interests of society demand that our present Election Act shall be changed, and that provision shall be made so that our women shall have a voice and a fair share in the government of the country. Further than that, I also wish to say that, if some provinces of Canada lag behind in the matter of granting the franchise to the women of those provinces, it makes it all the more imperative on this Parliament and Government to see that equal justice is done to the women of all the provinces of Canada. The old system, under the present Election Act, of using the provincial voters' lists, is, under present conditions, an absolute impossibility, if we are to have equality and justice extended to the whole people of Canada. If, for none of the reasons which I have so feebly endeavoured to advance, or if the chivalrous instincts of every hon. gentleman in this House do not compel -him to vote for the measure now before the House, let me say, if for none of these, then for very shame's sake let us remove the stigma and reproach of despotism from pur escutcheon. Let us prove ourselves worthy of the compliment that was paid us by that great French statesman who was with us on Saturday last, M. Viviani, when he stated that the sons of Britain, wherever they go, bring emancipation and liberty with them. I beg leave to move the adoption of the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to endorse the motion of the member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), let me at the outset say that I am well aware that a great difference of opinion prevails among the male voters of Canada as to the wisdom of granting the

franchise to our momen. I am no new *convert to the principle of allowing the ladies to have the vote. A proposal was made last year, and a similar proposal has been made during this session, that the women of certain provinces be given the right to vote. I am opposed to the idea of singling out a particular province that may have granted to its women the right of the franchise. I believe that the women of the whole of the Dominion are entitled to the franchise; more than that, I believe that11 they have always been entitled to it. I have been in public life for upwards of thirty years and, having given some thought and attention to this subject, I never could see the justice of men arrogating to themselves the sole right to vote.
What are the objections that are urged against granting women the franchise? We are told that the women should stay in the home. Well, I think that a little break in the monotony of the lives of our wives and mothers would not be any very great detriment to them, to the homes that they live in, or to the people with whom they work from day to day. When I think of the devotion to duty of our women; when I think of the wives of the labourers and the farmers, getting up betimes, even before the stars disappear, or working into the weary hours of night, I realize that they well deserve the franchise, and should always have had it.
We are told, too, that woman is the weaker vessel; that the men have to do the fighting. Well, since when have we adopted a system of avoirdupois in qualifying men to vote? Do we weigh them on the scale, measure the size of their biceps, wrists, ankles, fists, and so on, in order to determine whether they shall have a vote? If we did, where would the Minister of Trade and Commerce be? I am afraid that he would be entitled to only half a vote, and that the right hon. leader of the opposition would be entitled to only three-quarters of a vote. As to the Solicitor General-well, I would hardly like to say just what portion of a single vote he would be entitled to. My idea is that there are just as good brains in the heads of our women as there are in those of the men, and it does not make very much difference whether the head is covered by a creation from a millinery shop or whether the top piece was purchased in a gents' furnishing store. Among the thoughtful men of our country who have considered the question and who are animated by a

spirit of fairness, there has been a willingness to grant to our women the right to vote. The only thing lacking, I think, has been the expression of a well-defined desire for jt on the part of the ladies themselves. It is true that we have a number of women in this country who disclaim any desire to have a vote. Such women have not had the opportunity of cultivating any taste for exercising the franchise. How did the men learn political games; how did they learn to take part in politics? Simply by exercising their right to vote, and the same effect which resulted from the exercise of the franchise by men would follow from giving the vote to the ladies. They will think about these things; they will study them just as the men did, and bye-and-bye they will exercise the franchise with just as great a measure of intelligence.
I was in a house not very long ago in which the younger members of the family and the father were discussing the question of votes for women. The young men and the young women said: mother does not want to vote; she does not care anything about it. Well, when I thought of the poor mother and the opportunities she had had of studying this question, I came to the conclusion that it was not much wonder that mother had no taste for exercising the franchise. I do say that it would make a very desirable break in the usual routine of her life if she was allowed to exercise the franchise and was compelled to step out of the rut into which may years of hard work had placed her.
I believe in the equality of men and women. While a divine and beneficent Providence has not created them exactly alike, or intended that they should follow the same sphere of life, each has been given a work to do. With regard to the enactment and enforcement of laws which affect them so vitally, the women have just as much right to have a vote in public affairs as the men have.
Now, how can this be done? I believe it would toe found necessary to have a Dominion-wide franchise. We ought to have a Dominion voters' list that would cover all parts of the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific. We are met with the objection that this would be expensive, that it would cost more than the present system. As one who has been connected with municipal life during a great many years, and who has a working knowledge of such matters as they affect the province of Ontario, I want to say that the present system costs just as much as the proposed system would cost.

I have had experience with voters' lists under iboth systems. The only difference would be that under a Dominion-wide franchise the expense of the compilation of a voters' list would fall upon the Dominion, whereas under the present system it falls upon the municipalities and upon those who are seeing that the lists are properly prepared. One system, then, is just as expensive as the other. One lamentable defect in connection with the compilation of the voters' list in the organized parts of the province from which I come is that, inasmuch as we usually hold our elections in the late summer, or in the fall, the voters' lists that we use are practically a year and a half old. A few years ago the late Mr. James Conmee, then member for Rainy River, introduced into this House a measure, which was duly passed, empowering the Dominion Government to compile the voters' lists.
So that we have in the part of the country in which I live, in some of the townships which are not yet organized, the anomaly of having the Government compile a voters' list, and that method seems to work out all right there. Frequent compilations appear a little unnecessary if two elections take place in close succession, but if they are a year apart there ought,to be some method of getting the voters' list more up to date. In the hack-woods of Ontario, in those townships that are not yet organized, the voters' lists are more up to date than in the organized parts of the country where many thousands of men, who have moved away or who have come of age after the assessment lists have been made out, are deprived of the right to vote. Some method, therefore, ought to be devised to bring the lists up to date so that when an election comes every one will have an opportunity of exercising the franchise. I think that can best be done by having a Franchise Act passed by this Parliament and the compilation of our voters' lists placed in the hands of some branch of the Service.
The general trend of affairs has been towards extending the franchise to women. Every hon. member is aware that the storms that sweep over this country generally commence in the broad regions of the Pacific and move in an easterly direction, and this storm, if I may call it such, that has arisen has come from the far west and is sweeping eastward so that it will not be long before the ladies have the vote throughout the whole Dominion, and I think we should bring about that result by enactment of
this House so that no stumbling block may be thrown in the path of this movement. British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario have passed legislation for votes for women. The suffrage has been extended to women in Australia, New Zealand, the Isle of Man, Finland, Norway, Denmark, Iceland, Yucatan, and the women have municipal suffrage on the same terms as men throughout the British Isles and in Sweden, and a certain measure of municipal franchise rights in some of the British possessions, such as the city of Belize, in British Honduras, Rangoon, Burmah, and Baroda and Bombay in British India. In the United States, the women possess the franchise on equal terms with men at all elections in Wyoming, since 1869; in Colorado, since 1893; in Utah, since 1896;	in Idaho,
since 1896; in Washington, since 1910; in California, since 1911; in Arizona, Kansas and Oregon since 1912, and in Nevada and Montana since 1914. In the year 1913, the Territorial Legislature of Alaska granted full suffrage to women. Under the state law of 1913 in Illinois, it was construed that women could vote for Presidential Elector, members of the State Board of Equalisation; Clerk of the Appellate Court, County Collector, County Surveyor, members of the Board of Assessors, members of the Board of Review, Sanitary District Trustees and all the officers except police magistrates, of cities, villages and towns, and so on. Women have the right to vote in regard to matters connected with the schools, etc., in Connecticut,' Delaware, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Vermont, Wisconsin and Alaska, which I mentioned before. In Iowa, the women may vote at all school or municipal elections upon any proposition to vote bonds or increase the tax levies. Viewing the question from every standpoint, I consider that the general trend throughout the world is in the direction of extending the franchise to women; I do not know of a single country that, after adopting and trying out woman suffrage, has since discarded it, and I think we shall be quite safe in this country of ours in putting upon the Statute Books a law whereby women and men shall have equal rights in regard to the franchise. I trust, therefore, that this Parliament will see its way clear to place upon the Statute Books of this country a law

extending equal franchise rights 4 p.m. to every woman in every province of the Dominion.
As mentioned by the mover of this resolution, we have in this country a large number of people from foreign lands, many of whom know practically nothing of the affairs of this country, who have not the same ideals that we have, who come from a different civilization from ours and who apparently place no value on the franchise except what may he expressed in a form that may be very objectionable, and that I will not discuss in this House. Under such circum-istances, we ought to discriminate; and if I had my way, speaking for myself, I certainly would have 'an educational test, but I know that would meet with objections from men on both sides of the House. I think, however, that some educational test ought to be applied before we grant the franchise to any one whether he comes from Canada or from some foreign land because I submit that before a person receives the tremendous power of the franchise, he ought to be able to read and write in one of the official languages of Canada and know something of the affairs of this country. In Germany, I believe the franchise is based upon property qualifications; a man there exercises his franchise according to his financial condition; if he is worth a hundred thousand dollars, his vote is worth perhaps a hundred time3 as much as a man who has ten dollars. In that way the wealth of the country commands the situation, and that probably is primarily responsible for the great world struggle in which we are now engaged, because the common, every-day people of Germany have very little voice in determining what the country shall do. I believe we would escape from that result by granting equal franchise rights in every part of Canada; one man or one woman, one vote. The franchise that prevails in one province should prevail in every province, and the ladies should be put on an equal footing with the men. I heartily endorse the resolution moved by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland).

Mr. Speaker, it will perhaps be remembered that at the last session of Parliament I moved a resolution having in view the removal of the anomaly which now undoubtedly exists in the different provinces in respect to the right of women to vote for members of this House. I am not quite sure whether in order to

have the views which I entertain properly presented to the House, it may not be advisable for me to move an amendment to the motion of my hon. friend, because there is a possibility that the motion, which I have renewed at the present session and which stands upon the Order Paper with some alterations and in some wider language than my resolution of last year contained, may be deemed to be out of order under the rule of the House which prevents the same subject matter being twice considered.
I would suggest to my hon. friend who has made the motion and to the leader of the Government, whether it might not be better for my motion to be incorporated in some way with that of the hon. gentleman, and then if it were passed by the House it would be an expression of opinion that the anomaly should be done away with by placing the women of Alberta and Saskatchewan in the same position as the women of Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia, or if that were not deemed desirable, the Government could introduce legislation to extend the franchise to women subject to such limitations as Parliament might impose.
Where does the difference-come in between the two motions that my hon. friend refers to?

The difference comes in in this way. The motion now before the House simply recommends to the Government the extending the franchise to women all over Canada. The motion is very general in its terms; it is not definite, but simply urges that the question of extending the Franchise to women should engage the attention of the Government during the present session. Now, my resolution is more definite in form; it declares that the anomaly existing as to the right to vote between the women of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta and those of the other three provinces where the women are granted the franchise should be done away with, or a general law be introduced.

Would my hon. friend
mind explaining the anomaly he refers to?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I should be very glad if my hon. friend would go into' that pretty fully, because the view which fie set forth is not the view entertained by the Minister of Justice or the Solicitor General.

I am glad my right hon. friend has drawn my attention to that. I

think the House has been somewhat in the dark as to the opinion of the Minister of Justice on the subject ever since a question was put to him in the session of 1916 as follows:
Q. Is it the opinion of the Minister of Justice that women who are on the voters' list in the province of Manitoba, which province has granted the franchise to women, will be entitled to vote for members of the House of Commons?
The Minister of Justice replied:
It has never been the practice to answer questions of law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is quite correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman question that?

I do on a matter of this kind. I would think that the Minister of Justice ought to advise Parliament as to how the law stands on the subject. If the Minister of Justice is not to advise Parliament on questions of law, upon what subject is he to advise Parliament? Surely not on financial matters, or agricultural matters, or matters affecting the Department of Marine and Fisheries, for these belong to the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I would rather suppose upon a question such as this, which has excited so much public attention and which is almost vital for the women of Manitoba, British Columbia, and Ontario to be informed upon, that when a member of Parliament asks the Minister of Justice in the House as to how the law stands in the matter, it would be only reasonable for him to give his view, because undoubtedly his view would be the view of the Government. The Minister of Justice must advise somebody. Even to-day I presume the question must be up before the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery in connection with the printing of the voters' lists. I presume that the lists for Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, if not Ontario as well, are now in the office of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. If the local officials have done their duty, those lists must contain the names of those women who under the provincial laws are entitled to the provincial franchise. It is the duty of those officials to include all provincial voters on the lists which they send to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, and then it is right up to the Minister of Justice, I would say, to advise the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery as to whether under the Dominion law he must erase from those lists the names of all women voters; that is a question which I would suppose the Minister of Justice must decide. However, the Minister of Justice must be the judge of that. I will invite him now, however, or before this discussion is through, to advise the House as to whether or not the women of Manitoba, Ontario and British Columbia are entitled to vote for members of this Parliament by reason of their being on the provincial lists.
I do not see very well how the Minister of Justice can avoid giving an opinion upon a question of that kind.
From the study which I have given to the Dominion Elections Act, I have come to the conclusion, and I give it for what it is worth, that women who are on the provincial voters' lists for the three provinces of Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia, are entitled to vote for members of the House of Commons; I think there can be no doubt about that. Nor can there be any doubt, I think, that women to-day are entitled to be candidates for the House of Commons and become members, if the people desire to elect them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In all the
provinces?
In all the provinces.
Women are not on the list in the province of Ontario, and cannot be put on, the list except by legislation of this Parliament.

Yes, I think it would be ultra vires of the provincial legislature. It seems to me this Parliament must say as to whether or not women should have the right to vote for members of this House. Section 69 of the Dominion Elections Act declares the qualifications of candidates, and will be found on page 17 of Volume 1 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906. It says:
Except as in this Act otherwise provided, any British subject may be a candidate in an election for a seat in the House of Commons.
These words are as broad as words can be. It will not be denied that women are British subjects, and in the list of disqualifications there is no provision that the candidate must be a male.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Might I ask a question purely for information? Upon what ground does my hon. friend base the proposition that women can be candidates for the House of Commons, but that they cannot vote?

The language is different in the two statutes, no doubt, but is it sufficiently different to justify the distinction the hon. gentleman has drawn?
That is, as to Alberta and Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
But as to the
others?

As to these, no distinction. That is my contention. In Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia, there having been created a provincial franchise, and the names of those entitled to vote being placed on the provincial voters' list, these parties are, by that very act, entitled to vote for members of this House. But it happens that, in the cases of Alberta and Saskatchewan, the Dominion Elections Act limits the right to vote to male persons.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: So far as I know, the view expressed by the hon. member is a novel one, and I desire to know whether I follow his argument correctly. As I understand it, the hon. gentleman is of opinion that in all the provinces of Canada women have the right to become candidates at elections for this House?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Then, on what does he base the distinction, which he evidently draws, between their right to become candidates at elections for this House, and their right to vote at an election for this House? He does not admit that they have the right to vote in every province. The distinction he makes must be based on a comparison of the legislation in one case and in the other.

In the provinces until recently only the names of male persons could be placed upon the voters' lists. That was a limitation in the provincial law. Therefore, not being on the provincial lists, they could not vote for members of the House. But recently the legislatures of Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia have altered their laws and have struck out the word " male," so that a British subject, whether male or female, having the qualifications of residence and age, is entitled to vote for a member of the provincial House, and therefore is placed on the provincial list. Having got that far, we come to the Dominion Elections Act, which many years ago adopted the provincial lists as the lists upon which the election of members of this House shall be run. Now, my view-and I am absolutely

clear upon it-is that women in all these provinces of Manitoba, Alberta, Saskatchewan, British Columbia and Ontario, their names being upon the provincial voters' lists, are entitled to vote for members of this House unless there are some disqualifying words in the Dominion Elections Act. But there are these disqualifying words as to Saskatchewan and Alberta, though not as to any other province.
Let me ask the patience of hon. members while I call their attention to the provisions of the law affecting this matter. Some persons reading the Dominion Elections Act and seeing the masculine '* he" or "him" in many seetious, might assume that that fact alone would indicate that Parliament intended in all the provinces to limit the vote to male persons. But that does not follow, because of the Interpretation Act, which will be found in the Revised Statutes on page 8, section 31, paragraph (i) it is provided:
Words importing the masculine gender include females.
Therefore no inference is to be drawn from the masculine term. The word "he," if the context permits it, means also "she," and "him," would mean "her" just as much as if the feminine term had been used. Now, I call attention to the Dominion Elections Act, section 2-the interpretation section- paragraphs (d) and (e):
"Elector" or "voter" means any person entitled to vote at an election under the provisions of this Act.
(e) "Voters' list," or "list of voters," includes any official list of persons entitled to vote at an election, and, when provincial lists are referred to, includes any official list of persons entitled to vote at a provincial election.
Now, we come to Part I of the Dominion Elections Act. Section 5 sets forth the following limitation:
This part dos not apply to the Provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta or to the Yukon Territory.
And section 6 provides:
For the purposes of any Dominion election held within the limits of a province, the voters' lists shall, except as herein otherwise provided, be those prepared for the several polling- divisions established, and which on the sixtieth day next preceding the day fixed for the nomination of candidates for such Dominion election, were in force, or were last in force, under the laws of that province, for the purposes of provincial elections.
And section 12 is as follows:
Within ten days after the final revision of every list of voters for the purposes of provincial elections, and within ten days after

any change or alteration in or substitution tor any such list under the provincial law, it shall he the duty of the custodian thereof to transmit to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, by registered mail, a copy of such list or change of alteration therein, or substituted list, as the case may be, certified under the hand of such custodian, and having every alteration, addition, or erasure therein identified by his initials.
I think it is absolutely clear that it is the duty of the local official, within ten days after the final revision of the list of voters for the purpose of a provincial election, to transmit to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery simply the list of voters entitled to vote for members of the Provincial Legislature.
Under the provincial laws as they are today in those five provinces, those lists must include all the voters whether they are male or female. Every man and every woman entitled to vote for members of the provincial legislature must be on those provincial lists and those lists must be transmitted to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. Section 14 says:
For the purposes of Dominion Elections, such certified copy shall be deemed to be the original and legal list of voters for the polling division for which the list of which it is a copy was prepared, so long as that list remains in force, subject, however, to such changes and additions as are, subsequent to revision, made in such list under the provisions of the provincial law.
Section 19 makes provision for any changes which have been made in the voters' lists since the final revision, being added to the original lists. Section 21 provides:
So long as and whenever, for any reason, a certified copy of any list of voters as finally revised has not been transmitted to or received by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, pursuant to the provisions of this Act, the original and legal list for Dominion elections shall be the same as that for provincial elections.
You see, Mr. Speaker, that in. the sections to which I have referred there is no limitation as to whether voters are male or female.

Would the hon.
gentleman state where he gets his legal sanction for a woman being a candidate?

I gave that. Perhaps
my hon. friend was not in when I quoted from the Dominion Elections Act, section 69. I hope I will be pardoned, Mr. Speaker, for digressing a little from the consideration of the law relating to the voters' lists to answer my hon. friend. He will find that by section 69 it is provided:
Except as in this Act otherwise provided, any British subject may be a candidate in an election for a seat in the House of Commons.
No one will deny that a woman is a British subject or may be a British subject just as much as a man, or that if a woman is born within the British Empire, or becomes naturalized, she is a British subject just as much as a man.
The legal right is not based on the fact of being on the voters' list, then?

Not at all. A person
may be a candidate although not on the voters' list. There used to be a property qualification for candidates for Parliament, but that has been done away with and a free choice is left to the electors to elect whomsoever they please in the House of Commons, irrespective of qualification. However, there are some disqualifications which will be found in section 70 but which I need not refer to because that section has no bearing on the question of the right of a woman to be a candidate for Parliament.
Now, I have shown to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is no limitation whatever in Part I of the Dominion Elections Act, which applies generally throughout Canada, which would prevent women from having the right to vote provided they are on the provincial list. The sole condition, speaking in general terms, which the Dominion Parliament has imposed is that they shall be upon the provincial list. Then, to repeat my argument, it is that unless in the Dominion statute itself we find some disqualification, some limitation, of the right to vote for the House of Commons, every person., whether male or female, who ie on the provincial voters' list and is entitled to vote for a member of the provincial legislature in any of the provinces, may also vote for members of the House of Commons. If there were no limitations in the Dominion Elections Act in regard to two of the provinces of Canada, I would not have spoken to-day, I would not have presented my resolution, I would not have brought this matter before this House.
. Now, Mr. Speaker, I will call your attention to Part II of the Dominion Elections Act which deals especially with the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta and the Yukon Territory. The first section to which 1 shall refer is section 3, which provides that this part of the Act applies exclusively to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta and the Yukon Territory. Then section 32 says:
In the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, except as in this Act otherwise provided, every male person shall be qualified to vote at the

election of a member under this Act, who, not being an Indian, is a British subject and of the full age of twenty-one years, and has resided in either of the said provinces for at least twelve months, and, in the electoral district where he seeks to vote, for at "least three months, immediately preceding the issue of the writ of election ; Provided that, except as hereinafter provided, an elector may only vote at the polling station of the polling division in which he is a resident at the time of voting.
There is the same provision with respect to the Yukon. Section 33 says:
In the Yukon Territory, save as in this Act otherwise provided, every male person shall be qualified to vote at the election of a member under this Act, who, not being an Indian, is a British subject and of the full age of twenty-one years-

Can my hon.
friend tell us why that limitation was put in the Act?

No, I cannot. It would be very difficult to say with certainty what influenced Parliament at that time. It probably was that there were no provincial lists and Parliament was called up,on to create a franchise as to these provinces. In the judgment of Parliament at that time it was thought desirable to only give the vote to male persons. I presume that was the reason. No doubt, the different provinces entertained the same view with regard to their provincial lists and I think in all of them it will be found that until recently the word " male " was used instead of simply the word " person ", so that the right of the franchise was limited to males. I can think of no other reason than that which influenced Parliament. To make it absolutely clear that only males can vote in Saskatchewan and Alberta, I wpuld call attention to the form of instructions to voters which will be found on page 82:
Information for Electors.
The following is the qualification of electors as prescribed by the Parliament of Canada:-
Every male person shall be qualified to vote at the election of a member under this Act who, not being an Indian, is a British subject, and of the full age of twenty-one years, and who has resided in the [province of Saskatchewan or Alberta, or the Yukon Territory (or as the case may be,) for at least twelve months immediately preceding the issue of the writ of election].
Then provision is made for the oath which the elector may be required to take in those provinces. It will be found at page 89. It is as follows:
You do swear that you are of the male sex and a British subject, that you are not an Indian, that you are of the full age of twenty-one years and that you have resided in the province of Saskatchewan or Alberta or the Yukon Territory (as the case may be) for at least 
twelve months, and (in case of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta) in this electoral district for at least three months, immediately preceding the issue of the writ of election, and that you are now resident in this polling division.
I can not think that there is any doubt about the right of women, if their names are on the provincial lists in the provinces of Manitoba, Ontario and British Columbia, to vote for members of this House. Neither can I think there is any doubt that the disqualification contained in part two of the Dominion Elections Act as to Saskatchewan and Alberta will prevent the women of those two provinces from having the same right which the women of Manitoba, Ontario and British Columbia will have. The question is, should that anomaly be done away with? In considering this question, it seems to me we have to bear in mind that a great many years ago, in 1898, the General Dominion Franchise Act was repealed and it was provided that the provincial lists should be the lists which would govern in elections for the Dominion House. Parliament then came to the conclusion that it would be desirable to entrust the preparation of the lists to the local authorities, and that the Dominion elections should be run upon provincial lists. That has continued to be the law from that time to the present. It has been thought that it was in the best interest of the country to have the elections run upon the provincial lists. If that is a correct view to take, and it seems to have been regarded as correct by both of the great political parties of this country for a period of nineteen years, then it seems to me that there should be uniformity. It would be a strange anomaly that, of the persons who are on the provincial lists and entitled to vote for members of a provincial House and who, except for an express disqualification contained in a Dominion statute, would all be equally entitled to vote for members of this House, the women of two provinces of this Dominion should be debarred by the law of this House from that right, while the women of three other provinces, being in the same identical position so far as the provincial lists are concerned, should have the right to vote for members of this Parliament. Let me repeat that, in respect to the provincial legislatures, the women of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Ontario and British Columbia are in exactly the same position; they are entitled

to vote for the members of the provincial legislatures. They are entitled to be on the provincial lists. It is the duty of the local authorities to transmit their names as provincial voters to the Clerk of the Grown in Chancery, and, under tfhe law, it will be his duty, or if not his duty it will be the duty of the returning officer if the law is allowed to remain as it is, to strike the names of women voters off the provincial lists of the two provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and to leave them on the provincial lists for the three provinces of Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia. It is that anomaly which I think ought to be removed. I think the conditions of the franchise may well be left, as they have been during the past nineteen years, to the provincial legislatures. The law has worked very satisfactorily, and I see no reason why there should be ia change.

Is the hon. member aware that under the Provincial Act in Ontario the lists are prepared only shortly before a general election in that province, and that, therefore, those lists could not be forwarded here, except in a year in which an election in that province bad occurred, and that we could not compel the provincial authorities to prepare a last when we were going to have a general election for this House?

That would depend on
when there would be a general election.

The federal election
would have to come in the same year as the provincial election.

It might be that this
year, if there was an election 'before the provincial lists could be forwarded here, the election might have to be run on the lists of last year. But after next year, when women will be on the provincial lists in Ontario, there will always be a provincial list with the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery here containing the names of women, on which list a Dominion election would be held, and these women would be entitled to vote. Whether the names of all women would be properly on the list is another question; but in Ontario women would be entitled to vote just as men are entitled to vote.
In the motion which I have placed on the Order Paper, which is definite in its character, I would say, with the permission of the House, that I ask the House to declare specifically either that the disqualification contained in part two of the Dominion Elections Act as to the women of Saskatchewan and Alberta, should be done away with, or that they should all be put on the same footing, and that the women of other provinces whose names are on the provincial lists should be placed in exactly the same position. Or, if that should be deemed by the House not to be desirable, then that Parliament itself should grant the franchise to women, subject to such limitations as may be thought desirable. If my hon. friend (Mr. Sutherland), upon consideration, would consent to incorporate the resolution which I have had the honour to submit to the House with his own, that, I think, would enable the members of this House to express their views, if it is their opinion that this absurd anomaly should be done away with. It would enable members generally who are in favour of granting to women the right of franchise, to say that it should be done in either one way or the other. I cannot help thinking that if the franchise were still left with the provincial legislatures it would be better. Neither can I help thinking that if, as the result of so leaving it to the provincial legislatures and doing away with this anomaly as it exists in Saskatchewan and Alberta, the franchise should be granted to the women of all five provinces, the legislatures of the four remaining provinces, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island-when they would see that the legislatures of the other five provinces had given women the right to vote for provincial legislatures, and thereby, ex necessitate, for members of the House of Commons, would not be long in following suit and extending to women in those four provinces the same right to vote for members of provincial legislatures, and, as a result, for members of this House. I would suggest to my hon. friend, if I may be permitted to do so without being out of order, that instead of pressing his resolution, which is a very admirable one except that it is too general in its terms and too indefinite, and that it does not commit the House, or, if it is passed, does not commit the Government to anything except that they should give the matter attention-I would suggest that he strike out of his resolution all the words after the word "that," and substitute my resolution as follows:
That, whereas, in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, the provincial franchise has "been granted to women by legislative enactment, and in British Columbia the electors

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will do so later.

Perhaps it might be also understood, as I do not wish to prolong my remarks, that if such an arrangement could not be agreed to, I might be permitted later to move an amendment, after having heard from my right hon. friend, without making any further remarks. To keep myself in order, I will move the following amendment, with the understanding that I shall withdraw it if my hon. friend who has moved the resolution will agree to incorporate in it the resolution which I have upon the Order Paper:
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
The Dominion Elections Act should be so amended at the present session as to make uniform the right of women to vote for members of the House of Commons in those provinces which have granted to them the provincial franchise.
This amendment is along the lines that I have endeavoured to direct the attention of the House to as being the most desirable. I would prefer that we should agree upon a unanimous resolution in favour of extending to women the right, to which they are clearly entitled.
I was exceedingly pleased to hear the hon. gentleman who moved the resolution
[Mr. Pugsley.I
and my hon. friend who seconded it speak so strongly in favour of conferring the franchise upon women. The only respect in which I differ from them is in their argument that instead	of adhering
to the provincial franchise, this Parliament should adopt a general Franchise Act. This would mean dealing with the franchise generally, and not alone with the immediate subject which we aTe called upon to deal with. One hon. gentleman has said that a good many people in this country are opposed to extending the franchise to women. That assertion presents a very strong reason in favour of leaving the matter to the provincial legislatures. The extension of the franchise is a matter of education, and the safest way to deal with it is to leave it to the provincial legislatures, which are the best judges of the sentiments of the people in the particular provinces which they represent. I am sure that in the long run this method would result in greater satisfaction and better legislation.
I do not intend to argue at any length in favour of extending the franchise to women; I think that the time for argument has passed. The action of the most civilized countries in the world in granting this measure of justice to women ought to be convincing to this Parliament that it is the right thing to do. The fact that the great provinces of Ontario, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia have, either with perfect unanimity or by an almost unanimous vote, granted the franchise to women, ought to be a convincing argument to this Parliament that it is the right thing to do. The fact that in the United States 149 women belong to the Electoral College, that 7,000,090, in round numbers, is now the total of the women's vote, and that other strides have been made there in granting the suffrage to women, ought to be convincing proof that no evil has resulted from granting to women the franchise. The hon. gentlemen who have spoken in support of the resolution have pointed out ihat it would be impossible to overestimate the tremendous sacrifices which the women of Canada have made in the great struggle in which we are now engaged. Their sacrifices have been great, but, what is of equal importance, their work has been intelligent. They have combined skill and judgment with patriotic devotion to their country; they have given magnificent service, which has done a great deal to enable Canada to take the noble part which she is taking in this great war. Shall it be said that the women who have shown such in-

telligence, such good judgment, such energy, such devotion to their country, shall not be permitted to say how their country shall be governed; shall not he permitted to take any part in the direction of its affairs? As I have said, the time for argument has passed, and to-day the burden is upon those who hold that the franchise should not be granted to women. I do hope that this House will express the opinion that the Government should, at the present session, bring down a measure which will wipe out the disqualification of women so far as the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan are concerned, and will give to those women whose right to the franchise has been recognized by their legislatures the same right which their sisters in the other provinces of Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia have; that the women, in all the provinces upon whom the provincial franchise may be conferred shall, by virtue of that fact, their names being on the provincial voters' lists, have the right to vote for members of the Dominion Parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Is my hon.
friend in favour of extending the franchise to the women of all the provinces or only those in which the franchise has been extended to them by the provincial legislatures?

I would leave the provincial franchise to govern just as now. I think it would be proper to do so. It may be said that this Parliament ought to throw around the extension of the franchise to women certain restrictions; that they ought to extend it to women who are unmarried and to women who have property. To that I say, No. If we are going to extend the franchise to women, we ought to do what the provincial legislatures have done, that is, place them on an equal footing with men. We ought to give to every woman, married or single, possessing the qualification of residence the same as is required in respect of men, the same right to vote as a man has. While the British people have moved along pretty rapidly in the direction of woman suffrage, after a very hard struggle they have fixed the age at thirty years.
Twenty-five years.

Thirty years, I think it is. That strikes me as absurd. Mr. Lloyd George, the Prime Minister, in receiving a delegation of women recently in England, stated that the extension of the franchise
had been a matter of compromise, and he also called attention to the absurdity of fixing the extreme age limit of thirty years instead of fixing the same age as for men, but he said that no doubt very soon the anomaly would be done away with.
Do you think few women would vote if the age limit were thirty years?
Will the hon. member say why, having dilated upon the absolute right of women to vote, he proposes by his amendment to exclude women in certain provinces?

The reason is very
simple; it is that Parliament has left to the provinces the right to say who shall exercise the franchise and who shall not.
Is that a justification?

The provinces have the right to say that no man shall be allowed to vote unless he owns one thousand dollars of real or personal property or unless he has a certain income. The provinces are given by this Parliament the absolute right to fix the conditions of the franchise. The provinces have the right to extend the franchise to the Indians.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is hardly the case. We have simply for the time being adopted the franchise conditions which the provinces have established. Nevertheless, this Parliament is and always has been invested with the fullest possible jurisdiction to determine who shall vote at elections of members of this House.

I grant that; I grant
at once that Parliament in its wisdom has determined that, upon the whole, the best judges are the provincial legislatures and that it is better to leave the question of the right of the franchise to the pro-
5 p.m. vincial legislatures. Whether rightly or wrongly, that has been the view of Parliament for the past nineteen years, and as I have said, under this law, one province, if the legislature chose so to enact, might prescribe property qualifications which might be entirely different from the qualifications in another province; one province might prescribe a condition of residence which might be entirely different from what was prescribed by the legislature of another province; but all the same, only those to whom the province gave the right of voting for the election of members to the provincial House would be

entitled to have their names placed upon the lists which would qualify them to vote for members of the Dominion Parliament. It is upon that ground, as I have pointed out, that the present law has worked with great satisfaction during the past nineteen years, that I would still continue to leave to the provincial legislatures the question of whether women should be on the voters lists or not.

Is it not a fact that a few years ago this Parliament expressed its dissatisfaction with the voters' lists provided by the provinces and exercised the right from that day to this of compiling the voters' lists over large parts of the province of Ontario, and I think, of some of the other provinces?

I think my hon. friend is mistaken as to that. I do not think Parliament, during the past nineteen years, has ever declared itself against depending upon the provincial franchise and using the provincial voters' lists, and it has certainly never taken any steps which would show any disapproval of the present law.

This Parliament did as
I have stated, and for years now, under the authority of this Parliament, the Dominion Government has been compiling the voters' lists in the northern parts of the province of Ontario.

My hon. friend is surely wrong in speaking in general terms. He is referring entirely to the unorganized districts of Ontario in regard to which it might be desirable to have special provisions. I shall not take up any further time, but shall conclude by moving the amendment which I have read, with the understanding, if my hon. friend prefers something different, I shall be glad to draw up another one along somewhat different lines.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Without giving a ruling on the amendment of the hon. member for St. John city (Mr. Pugsley) at this stage, as it is entirely new to me, I feel it my duty to point out that the hon. member has upon the Order Paper a resolution, No. 6, following this, and it seems to me that that resolution, although it is not the same in terms, is substantially the same as that which he j*ow submits by way of amendment. Bourinot, at page 301, says:
Nor is it regular to move as an amendment to a question a motion of which notioe has been given and which appears in its place on the Notice Paper.

If the amendment submitted by the hon. member for St. John is substantially the same as his notice of motion-and I am inclined to think it is^-his amendment would not be in order, in that it is not competent for him to do by an indirect method that which he cannot do directly. I merely point out to the hon. member that I am inclined to the view that his amendment is out of order, but as the debate will probably proceed for a time, I shall be able to give a more definite ruling before it is concluded.

I would like, Sir, if in
considering the question, you *would keep in mind the fact that the amendment simply expresses the one view without any reference to any proposed legislation of a wider scope.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It had not been my intention to take any part in the debate upon the motion moved by the hon. member for South Oxford, nor is it now my intention to deal with the merits of the question raised by that motion. I rise simply because the hon. member for St. John has expressed so insistent a desire for an expression of opinion upon my part upon the question of whether or not there exists that anomaly, to remedy which, I understand, is the purpose of the amendment which he has proposed. I might refer in the first place to his criticism of the answer which was given to the question put at the last session of the House as to what the opinion of the Minister of Justice was upon the question which arises upon his motion, namely, whether the fact that a certain province has conferred the electoral franchise on women, operated in view of the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act, to give women the right to vote in elections for the Dominion Parliament.
The hon. gentleman found fault that in response to that question the answer was given that it was not the practice to answer questions of law. The hon. gentleman would not dispute, surely, that that was a question of law nor that my answer stated the universal practice. He went on to suggest that it was the duty of the Minister of Justice to advise the House on questions of law, and he asked who is it that the Minister of Justice is to advise if not the House of Commons? He suggested that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery must at the present time under the direction of the Minister of Justice be proceeding to strike names off the provincial lists. I

would like very respectfully to say that in all these suggestions the hon. member for St. John is labouring under an entire misapprehension. If the hon. gentleman will look at the statutes governing the function of the Minister of Justice he will see that the Minister of Justice is constituted-I do not pretend to give the exact words- the legal advisor of the Government, and of the different departments of the Government-not the legal -advisor of the House of Commons.
Is not the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery an officer of one of the departments?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He is an officer of the House of Commons, and I think it is a very serious question whether it would be a proper thing for him to take upon himself to act upon the advice of the Minister of Justice alone, and to proceed under his direction to strike names off the voters' lists without the intervention of anybody else, because after all the Minister of Justice might sometimes, though not always, be a political partisan.. So far as I know no such procedure ever takes place. I did not come prepared to speak on this subject to-day, and I have not specially looked at the provisions with regard to voters' lists, but I would be surprised to learn that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, under anybody's advice or direction, strides names off the voters' lists. I speak subject to possible correction, but I think there is really no room [DOT] for correction when I say that I do not think there is vested in the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery any discretion to strike names off voters' lists. In the voters' lists as they come to us from the provinces, quite irrespective of the question of woman's franchise, there may be, and sometimes there undoubtedly are, large numbers of names of persons who are not qualified to vote in a Dominion election, but I do not know of any authority under which the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery can strike those names off.
In giving the answer I did last year, the well-established practice was followed. In saying that as Minister of Justice I am not the advisor of the House of Commons, I only repeated what I have heard said many, many times by my predecessor in this office. I am not quite sure but that when I first took office I myself suggested just what the hon. member for St. John has suggested this afternoon. But whether it was I that put forward that proposition or
another, I have the clearest possible recollection of the very distinguished gentleman who was my predecessor in office taking distinctly the position that he had no function to act as advisor to the House of Commons. We are all here as members of the House of Commons, and the opinion of the gentleman who happens to be Minister of Justice is worth just what it may be worth as the opinion of one lawyer sitting in this House, and I have no doubt, in fact I would anticipate, that any person seeking light on the law would give at least equal respect and consideration to the opinion of other members of this House as they would to my opinion. If the Minister of Justice be the legal advisor of the House of Commons, it would seem to follow that the House of Commons ought to accept and act upon his advice, and it would be confiding to a member of the Government very large powers indeed, if his office gave him the right to speak authoritatively to this House as to what the law was, and this House was under any obligation to accept his view. I fancy the hon. gentleman himself would not be prepared in this particular case, or generally, to accept as conclusive whatever view I might express.
I am quite willing to express to the House my view upon the question of law that arises in the case, but as I did not come with the intention of discussing this question, and indeed it is one that apparently would not have presented itself upon the motion of the hon. member for South Oxford, my hon. friend and the House generally will perhaps pardon me if I am not as clear and concise as I might otherwise have been in the setting forth of this opinion.
