The proposition of the hon. gentleman that an anomaly exists by reason of the fact that women in those of the older provinces where the legislature has conferred the franchise are now entitled to vote in Dominion elections, whereas in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan where the legislatures have also conferred the franchise on women they are not entitled to vote, is, I think, a mistaken one. He rests his proposition, if I followed his argument rightly, upon the terms under which the Dominion statute recognizes that the voting qualifications prescribed by the different legislatures shall be sufficient to confer the right to vote in a Dominion election, and upon the provisions which recognize that the voters' lists prepared by the provinces shall, subject to certain conditions which are not now material, be used

in Dominion Elections. I understand the hon. gentleman to base his contention on the fact that our statute, in describing tne qualifications of those entitled to vote, says that every person who is a British subject, and so forth, qualified to vote in provincial election, shall be qualified to vote in a Dominion election as well. His contention is that because the statute does not create a disability upon any particular class of person, that the words " every person " must be taken as including all persons of any kind or description, and I think he finds an added strength for that argument in the fact that in that portion of the Election Act which deals with the persons for which the Dominion itself provides the qualifications, the words used are, "every male person."
That part of the proposition of the hon. member with which I do not agree is this: he contends that because by the statute itself no distinction of persons is made, it follows that the word "person" is to be interpreted as including all kinds of persons, even those labouring under existing legal incapacity at the time of the passing of the statute. If I follow the hon. member, he contends that if that statute does not impose any disability, there is no need of that statute in any express way removing any previously existing disability. Now, previous to the enactment of the Dominion Elections Act, the Dominion determined its own franchise and made its own lists; and, for the purpose of determining what a "person " was with regard to that franchise and the making of the lists, we had a provision defining a " person " as being a male person. So that, under the provisions of an immediately pre-existing law dealing with the subject of the franchise, the law for which the present law was substituted, " person " for franchise purposes, was a male person and did npt include women. It- is not impossible that we may find there the explanation of the insertion of the words " male person " when this Parliament came to make an Act defining the franchise, which it does in that part that deals with the province of Saskatchewan and Alberta, where when dealing with the other provinces it was merely the provincial franchise as regards the question of qualification -and I insist a little upon that, because I think it is well to bear in mind that all that Parliament declared itself willing to accept from the province was that persons who had the qualifications which the
province described

Does the hon. minister
say that in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, as the Dominion law stands at present, a woman could vote in an election to this House by reason of the Franchise Act in either of those provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, I thought I had
made it clear that my view was that they would not be entitled tp vote in a Dominion election. Consequently, I say there is no anomaly, that their position as regards voting in the Dominion elections is the same as the position of wpmen in the provinces where the province has not recognized the right of women to vote.
I lay stress on the fact that the matter with regard to which our law declares the readiness of Parliament to accept the decision of the provincial legislature is the matter of the qualification which will entitle a person to vote. But there is nothing in our statutes which hands over to the legislature of the province the power to determine who is and who is not, for the purposes of the franchise, a " person." Parliament, when it used the word, used it, no doubt, with a clear understanding of its meaning. I am not going to suggest that in the abstract a woman is not a person. I would not dare to say it even if I thought it, which, of course, I do not. But I submit that " person " in the Act of 1906 means to-day what it meant when the law was enacted, and that there is no power in the legislature of any province to make the word " person " in that Act mean something different from what it meant at the time it was enacted. And I think the hon. gentleman will agree with me that there are words which, with regard to special enactment, as a matter of law, have a meaning sometimes broader and sometimes narrower than their meaning in ordinary parlance. My proposition is that in that statute of 1906, when the legislature said " every person " it meant every male person, and that because it was not creating any capacity to vote, but was dealing with a " person " from the point of view of voting, and did not confer a capacity upon people who, up to the time of that enactment, had not the capacity to vote, and that we are not justified, in the absence of clear provision by the legislator intimating his intention to create an entirely new class of persons with capacity to vote, in inferring that he meant to do that merely because he spoke of " every person." In other words, the legislator, when he was enacting how were to be determined the qualifications of persons entitled to vote, must have had in

contemplation those persons who at the time-and from all previous times-had been the only persons capable of voting at all.

Assuming what the hon. minister says to be correct, can he suggest any reason why Parliament, in dealing with Saskatchewan and Alberta, where they have no provincial lists, should have used the words " male person " and in dealing with the provincial lists which are provided for in some provinces, said simply " person?"

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think I can suggest an explanation of how that happened. But, even if I be not in a position to offer any explanation, I submit that, as a matter of law, if the word " person " standing by itself had at the time of that enactment a perfectly clear meaning excluding the idea of a female person, you could not, by mere inference from the fact that in this other portion of the Act the legislator used the words " male person," safely conclude that he meant to alter the meaning attached to the word " person " as it was well recognized to 'be at the time he used the word in connection with that particular subject matter.
In a moment I shall show to the hon. member an authority which I think he will recognize as a very respectable authority where precisely the same thing occurred and where, notwithstanding it having so occurred, it was held in England that the word "person," as applied to the Franchise Act, did not include a woman. We have to take it as the starting point that our Act limits itself to accepting the determination of the provinces as to qualifications. As far as these lists are concerned, it defines the lists but I do not think my hon. friend will find anything in that statute saying that the mere fact of a person being on the list makes of that person an elector. In fact, there are numerous persons on these lists who are not qualified to vote at our elections. The question, therefore, is not whether a woman is or is not an elector under the provincial statute. So far as qualifications are concerned, if the province changed the qualifications of a person, without this Parliament changing its law, such person would 'become qualified to vote at a Dominion election. But until this Parliament undertakes to say that some one who, for the purposes of the Act which it enacted, would not be a person within the meaning of the Act when it was enacted, has become a person and has become so entitled, the province cannot impose that person upon this Parliament as being recognized under the legislation of this Parliament as being a person capable of voting.

Would the Minister
of Justice say what right this Parliament has to define the status of the province in regard to that particular question? Has not this Parliament to take the definition as handed out by the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This Parliament is not under any obligation to take the enactment of the province in regard to the qualification of voters. This Parliament has absolute power to determine who shall vote in elections and if persons, who are upon the provincial lists and are recognized by the provincial authority, vote in a Dominion election, it is not because the province says so but it is because this Parliament has said: We will take over your list and make it ours. By simply being on the provincial list a man does not vote, properly speaking, because he is on that provincial list; he votes because this Parliament has taken that list over and made it the Dominion list. He votes because this Parliament has said that he may vote, and not because the legislature has said so. That is only one way that this Parliament takes, of exercising its absolute power to determine who shall vote in Dominion elections.
But if his name is on the list he can vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not necessarily.
If he is otherwise qualified under the Provincial Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are classes of disqualification in our own Act. For a number of years my own name stood upon the voters' list but I was disqualified from voting 'because I held an office that, under the Dominion Elections Act, disqualified me.
Those are personal disqualifications.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; so that the fact of your being on the list is not conclusive evidence that you are an elector.
If women are on the voters' list for Ontario, does the minister contend that these women cannot vote for Dominion elections?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is my view.
That they cannot vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That they cannot vote, that the mere fact of their being upon the list does not make them voters.
What is the difference between them and men?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Because every "person," within the meaning of our statute, who has the qualifications prescribed may vote, but my proposition is that a woman, within the meaning of our statute is not included within the meaning of "person."
What is a woman if she is not a person?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Within the meaning of the statute, I say. The hon. member can say hosts of funny, and amusing, things, if he wants to and he can suggest that I am saying that a woman is not a person, but what I am saying is that when the legislators said that every "person" might vote he did not say anything to the effect that a woman should vote. I will point out to my hon. friend an authority that I think he will not laugh at. He may say that I am wrong, he may feel justified in laughing at me, but when I show him this authority I do not think he will laugh at it.
I was not laughing at my hon. friend but rather at the suggestion that a woman is really not a person.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
finds it necessary to say "really not a person," whereas the hon. gentleman would be more correct if he quoted me as saying that a woman was not included in the word "person" within the meaning of the statute. That is all I was saying. I think I am quite safe in taking it as the starting point that at common law, woman was incapacitated frpm voting. And I think I am just as safe in taking it that, at common law, -woman is equally incapacitated from being a member of Parliament.
I understand the minister to mean that the word " person " in our Act must be interpreted in vieiw of the conditions that existed at the time the legislation was passed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Precisely, and in view of what the law understood to be a person from the point of view of the capacity to vote and what therefore we must assume Parliament understood when it used the word. I think I am perfectly safe in saying that at common law a woman was not capable of being a voter for a member of

Parliament. At common law- and I think this answers the hon. gentleman's suggestion about a woman being a candidate for this House-a woman was not capable of being elected to Parliament. My proposition is this, that that incapacity will only disappear in face of legislation absolutely and clearly removing it and to say simply that every " person " shall be entitled to vote in face'of the fact that there existed a positive incapacity in a particular class of persons, or persons of a certain kind, does not justify the conclusion that Parliament meant to create a new class of capable people.

The Ontario statute says that every person shall be entitled to be on the voters' list. It does not say "male and female;" it says "every person." Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that it does not include women and that under the provincial Act as it stands now women cannot vote in Ontario at a provincial election?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not familiar with the provision but I understand that previously the statute said " every male person " and that now the legislator has come in and said: I do not want to say "male person" but to make it clear now that I mean every person, male and female, I am striking that out. What we have got by that is the perfectly clearly evidenced intention of the legislature to exclude the idea of a male person. My proposition goes no further than this: that, unless there be such clearly expressed intention, I do not think there is room for serious dispute.
We have not the same distinction in our own statute in regard to Alberta and Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
At no time did we strike out the word "male" as used in any part of the statute. What happened in regard to our statute is that, with regard to the old provinces where Parliament was accepting the qualifications as prescribed by the provinces, it used the words "every person." In that portion of the Act where Parliament was enacting a Franchise Act of its own for Saskatchewan and Alberta, it used the words "every male person." And if I am not mistaken, that was subsequent legislation, not being enacted at the same time; it was not a matter of comparing the two sections one with the other and saying: Shall we use the word "person" here, and shall we use the words "male person" there? Because in one statute enacted subsequently to that portion of the law the words "male

person" are used, because Parliament sought to be even more clear and distinct, that does not modify the meaning of the word "person" used in previous legislation; whereas in the case of the provinces they are making subsequent legislation, and making a deliberate change, substituting one provision for another, and striking out the word "male," thus making the whole provision utterly nugatory, unless the change give capacity to women, as it could not mean anything else than that the legislature wanted to get rid of the limitation in regard to sex. But in our legislation there never was any getting rid of a limitation in the legislation that was being dealt with, which said "every person." When Parliament was making a Franchise Act, it made use of a defined' term, "male person," which was only following out and making perfectly clear the well accepted meaning of "person" up to that time.
I said that the question was not new, that I would be able to cite respectable authority, indeed I might say conclusive authority, in support of the propositions I have been setting forth. In England the question has arisen in two cases, the case of Chorlton against Lings, Law Reports, Common Pleas, page 374; and the case of Nairn against the University of St. Andrews, one of the Scotch universities, to be found in Appeal Oases 1909, page 147, House of Lords. The latter case is especially striking as dealing with a question as nearly as can be on all fours with the question we are considering here. In the case of Chorlton and Lings, what was held was that:
Women are not entitled to vote in the election of members of Parliament, because they are by reason of their sex subject to a "legal incapacity" within the meaning of the enfranchising clauses of the Representation of the People Act 1867. By section 3 of the Representation of the People Act 1867 it is enacted that "every man'' having certain qualifications shall be entitled to vote; and by Lord Romil-ly's Act it is enacted that in all future Acts words importing the masculine gender shall be deemed and taken to include females, unless the contrary is expressly provided.
Held, that the words "every man/ in the Representation of the People Act, did not include females, because what is necessarily implied from the language of an Act is "expressly provided," and the Legislature, in the Representation of the People Act, were dealing not with the description of persons entitled to vote, but with their qualification, and therefore used the word "man" in the sense of "male persons."

Hear, hear, that is not very much against our position.
95 i

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When it used the word "man" it was not dealing with qualifications, but with the description of persons entitled to vote, dealing with descriptions, not with qualifications; and so it used the word "man," although there is an express Statute saying that "man" includes woman.
No. Is not the language of the Interpretation Act: that the masculine shall include the feminine where the context requires it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not dealing with our Interpretation Act. Perhaps my hon. friend did not follow me when I read the provision.

Would the minister
kindly repeat it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is enacted that in all future Acts words importing the masculine gender shall be deemed and taken to include females unless the contrary is expressly provided.
Not unless the context otherwise requires, but unless the contrary is expressly provided and in the face of that, with a statute that says that every man should have a right to vote and no express provision to the contrary, the court held that for the purpose of the franchise it did not include women. The word " man " is treated as being the equivalent of our word " person" for general purposes. But the reason why it does not include woman is that according to inveterate usage, woman was incapable of voting, and that you could not assume, that by the mere use of a generic word as "man," or "person," Parliament intended to remove that general incapacity.
The other case is perhaps more absolutely similar to this case. There we are dealing with the word "person." and likewise with the effect of a person being on the specific list which is defined as being the list of persons entitled to vote. Perhaps before we pass to the other case I might give a citation or two from the remarks of the judges in the case I have been speaking of. Two reasons were given why the word "man" in that case did not include woman: First the subject matter and general scope of the language of the Reform Act showed that the word man was not intended to include woman, and second because at common law women were under a legal disability and were incapable of voting, a condition which the statute had not relieved. Justice Byles said that it was impossible to suppose that Parliament when

dealing with qualification and *with, qualification only, intended by the variation of a phrase to admi\ to the poll the other half of the population. Chief Justice Bovill said [DOT]I do not collect from the language of this Act that there was any intention to alter the description of the persons who were to vote, hut rather conclude that the object was to deal with their qualifications; and if so important an alteration of the personal qualification was intended to be made as to extend the franchise to women, who did not then enjoy it, and were in fact excluded from it by the terms of the former Act, I can hardly suppose that the Legislature would have made it by using the word man.
The case of Naim vs. the University of St. Andrews bears, perhaps, more directly upon our present question, because the word in question is "person," and the question passed upon is the effect of enabling women to be included in the class of persons which, under the existing law, had been declared capable of voting. The question was that of the right to vote for a member to represent the University of St. Andrews. Without going into the exact words, the qualification to vote for a member to represent the University of St. Andrews was that of being a member of the council. At the time that was enacted, women were apparently not entitled to be members of the council, just as, at the time of our enactment, neither in the provinces nor anywhere else were women entitled to vote. Subsequently, under authority conferred upon them by statute, the authorities of the university recognized to women the right to become graduates and thereby to become members of the council of the university. Women, therefore, found themselves absolutely within the exact description of what was a lawful voter entitled to vote for the representation of the university in Parliament. Yet the court held that they were not entitled to vote.
Would the minister give the citation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Law Reports, Appeal Cases 1909, page 147. Here is the description of what was a lawful voter:
''Every person whose name is for the time being on the register of the general council of such university, shall, if of full age, and not subject to any legal incapacity, be entitled to vote in the election of a member to serve in any future Parliament for such university in terms of this Act"; and by s. 28, sub-s. 2, the following persons shall be members of the general council of the respective universities: "All persons on whom the university to which such general council belongs has after

examination conferred" certain degrees, "or any other degree that may hereafter be instituted."
The report continues:
The appellants were five women graduates of the University of Edinburgh, and as such had their names enrolled on the general council of that university, and they claimed as graduates and members of the general council the right to vote at the election of a member of Parliament for the university.
Held (affirming the decision of the Extra Division of the Court of Session), that the appellants were not entitled to vote in the election of the parliamentary representative of the university.
There is no evidence of any ancient custom for women to vote in parliamentary elections.
Some of the things said by the judges in this case are startlingly applicable to the present question. Lord Loreburn says:
In regard to the alleged* right of voting the appellants assert that, if ancient records are explored, there is evidence of women having enjoyed this right, and no adequate ground for affirming a constitutional or common law disability on the score of sex; and, further, that the Representation of the People (Scotland) Act, 1868, taken with the Universities (Scotland) Act, 1889, and the ordinances made under the last-mentioned Act, do upon their literal constitution confer upon women, if they comply with the requirements, a right to vote for university members.
Now, my Lords, it may be that in the vast mass of venerable documents buried in our public repositories, some of authority, others of none, there will be found traces of women having taken some part in parliamentary elections. No authentic and plain case of a woman giving a vote was brought before your Lordships. A few equivocal cases were referred to. I was surprised how few. And it is the same in regard to judicial precedents. Two passages may he found in which judges are reported as saying that women may vote at parliamentary elections. These are dicta delivered from an ancient manuscript of no weight. Old authorities are almost silent on the subject, except that Lord Coke at one place incidentally alludes to women as being under a disqualification, not dwelling upon it as upon a thing disputable, but alluding to it for purpose of illustration as a matter certain. This disability of women has been taken for granted.
It is incomprehensible to me that any one acquainted with our laws or the methods by which they are ascertained can think, if, indeed, any one does think, there is room for argument on such a point. It is notorious that this right of voting has, in fact, been confined to men. Not only has it been the constant tradition, alike of all the three kingdoms, but it has also been the constant practice, so far as we have knowledge of what has happened from the earliest times down to this day. Only the clearest proof that a different state of things prevailed in ancient times could be entertained by a court of law In probing the origin of so inveterate an usage. I need not remind your Lordships that numberless rights rest upon a similar basis. Indeed, the whole body of the common law has no other foundation.

I will not linger upon this subject. If this legal disability is to be removed, it must be done by Act of Parliament. Accordingly the appellants maintain that it has in fact been done by Act of Parliament. They say that the Act of 1868, while confining to men the franchise described in other sections, adopts different language in s. 27, using in that section the word "persons." I agree that the word "persons" would prima facie include women. But, in speaking of "persons,'' this same section limits them to those who are "not subject to any legal incapacity." I cannot doubt that by this limitation, if not otherwise, are excluded all such persons as may by law be disabled from voting. Peers are excluded, as are women. So, also, are others.
If the word "persons" in s. 27 of the Act of 1868 is wide enough to comprise women, then they are shut out by the exception of those subject to a legal incapacity. If the word "persons" is not wide enough to include women, then there is nothing in any Act of Parliament that gives the smallest foothold for the appellants' contention.
I do not want to take up the' time of the House by reading citations, but I wish to read from Lord Ashbourne's opinion. He speaks of what the Legislature had in contemplation when it used the word "persons."
Then he says:	^
In 1868 the legislature could only have had male persons in contemplation, as women could not then be graduates, and also because the Parliamentary franchise was by constitutional principle and practice confined to men.
Now when the legislature said that every person on the register of the university should be entitled to vote, there is what the court said that that meant eveTy male person, because at that time no female persons were entitled to vote anywhere nor could they be graduates. When our Parliament said that every person that has the qualifications provided by the legislatures shall be entitled to vote, it necessarily excluded women because at that time and for all time previously, nobody had had women as voters in contemplation at all and women could not be on a provincial list. Lord Ashbourne continues:
The Appellants strongly relied on the use of the word "man" in some earlier sections dealing with counties or boroughs.
There is just the suggestion made here with regard to the use of "person" in one place and "male" person in another. In this they use" person " in one place and " man " in another.
Mr. PU'GSLEY: Does not the hon. minister think that makes it stronger, "person" in one place, and "male" in another?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There may be a shade of difference, but the difference of effect in
both instances must rest upon the contention that the use of different words necessarily implies different meanings, and I think that it is a pretty light shade of difference. If it is an inevitable conclusion that because in one place I use the word " person " and in another " male person ", I mean different things in the two places, the distinction is very finely drawn if I can say: Well, I used " person " in one place and " man " in another, and I meant just the same.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I
should just like to add two further citations before leaving the case of Nairn and the University of St. Andrews, to which I was referring when the House rose at six o'clock. Lord Ashbourne, after saying what I read before the House rose at six o'clock, in which he made it quite clear that he excluded a woman in that particular case on the ground that she was not a person within the meaning of the statute, went on to say:
I can, then, entertain no doubt that, when examined, "person" means male person in the Act. The parliamentary franchise has always been confined to men. and the word "person" cannot by any reasonable construction be held to be prophetically used to support an argument founded on a Statute passed many years later.
I do not think any language could be more directly applicable to the present case. To hold that within the meaning of the statute of 1906 "person" included a woman, we must hold that it was prophetically used to support an argument founded on a statute passed twenty years later.
I should also like to cite a few words from page 161 where Lord Loreburn says:
It would require a convincing demonstration to satisfy me that Parliament intended to effect a constitutional change so momentous and far-reaching by so furtive a process. It is a dangerous assumption to suppose that the-Legislature foresees every possible result that may ensue from the unguarded use of a single word, or that the language used in statutes is so precisely accurate that you can pick out from various Acts this and that expression and, skillfully piecing them together, lay a safe foundation for some remote inference.
Before passing from the English cases I might mention the case of Bebb and the Law Society, where the question was whether a woman was eligible under the statute providing for the admission of "persons" as solicitors or attorneys. It was there held that:

Before the passing of the Solicitors' Act, 1843, women were by the common law of England under a general disability, by reason of their sex, to become attorneys or solicitors. That disability can be, and is, proved by inveterate usage. It could not be removed by a mere interpretation of the clause, such as the Solicitors' Act, 1843, s. 48, which provides that words importing the masculine gender shall extend to a female. There is nothing in the Solicitors' Act, 1843, or any amending statute which can be construed as giving women any new right to become solicitors. The disability therefore continues, and the Law Society cannot admit any woman to their preliminary examination- with a view to her becoming a solicitor.
I refer to this in connection with what was said about the provisions of our Interpretation Act, where the masculine is intended to include the feminine. The quotation I have just cited is directly applicable in that regard. No doubt that the provision of our Interpretation Act would render it impossible for us to draw any inference from the words "he or him or his" being used throughout the Election Act in reference to an elector or a voter, but it leaves untouched the question of the meaning of the word "person" and it may be well to mention in passing that while we have a. section in our Interpretation Act which is intended to clear up what is meant by "person" it does not refer at all to the question of sex. It includes within the definition of "person" corporate bodies and companies and so forth, but does not touch one way or the other the question of what may be meant as regards sex in any particular statute by the word "person." So we have no statutory disposition as to the proper interpretation in this regard to be given to the word "person." In this case of Bebb which I think bears directly on the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John, that because our statute says that any British subject of 21 years of age may be a candidate, and therefore a woman may be a candidate, Lord Robert Cecil in opening the case quotes from Maitland's History of English Law, (and it is referred to later on with approval by the judges) as follows:
As regards private rights women are on the same level as men, though postponed in the canons of inheritance; but public functions they have none. In the camp, at the council board there is no place for them.
The learned counsel declares that he accepts that statement, but arguing as he was that a woman might be a solicitor, he goes on to claim that the words "public function" must be defined narrowly. It goes without saying that to be a candidate
IMr. Doherty.]
or member of this House, or to vote is a public function. It is hardly necessary to cite anything in support of that proposition. In view of what is conceded all round in all the cases to which I have referred, a woman at common law was not capable of voting, and merely because the statute used the terms "every person" it appears clearly impossible to conclude,' in the absence of any such expressed intention by the legislature, that it intended to remove entirely that disability, or as one judge says, "to add to the voting body the other half of the population which never had voted before." On the strength of these authorities I think one can safely say that the mere use of the word "person" does not justify one in assuming that it was intended to effect this far-reaching revolution.
One of the cases I have cited is directly applicable to the present question. The meaning of the word " person " used under analogous circumstances is under consideration, and that word it }s declared cannot by any reasonable assumption be held to be prophetically used to support an argument founded on a statute passed many years later. So here, to sustain the argument of the hon. member, we must look upon the word used at a time when everybody knew that when speaking of persons in connection with voting no one thought of women, as used prophetically, and Parliament -as having in mind that possibly at some future time somebody would so alter the law that a woman would become a person capable of voting, and intended then that at any such time in the remote future, which might never come, women were to he included in the word " persons " and entitled to vote.
As regards the argument that my' hon. friend has sought to make based upon the lists, I do not see that it leads to the conclusion that the hon. member has come to. The sections dealing with the lists and with voting provide -that the provincial lists shall be used and these come from the provincial officers as being the lists of voters entitled to vote at the various polling divisions. As I understand the procedure- I do not like to be too positive about it- but I do not think it is open to much question, the clerk of the Crown in Chancery has not the power to sit down and cut this man and that man off the list. He simply takes the list and gets it printed and then that becomes the list. But that does' not mean that everybody on that list is entitled to vote in a Dominion election. Among the affidavits required to be taken and for

which forms are provided, you will find one for the case of a man on the provincial voters' list who is disqualified under the Dominion statute. Sections 67 and 69 give quite a list of people who are disqualified under the Dominion Act. The procedure that is adopted is this: When a man who is on the provincial list presents himself to vote at a Dominion election he may then he sworn as to whether or not he is disqualified under the Dominion net, which demonstrates that being on the list is not conclusive of the right to vote, and that merely having his name on the list would not entitle some one who did not come within the designation of "person" within the meaning of the statute, to vote.
In our country we have had this question of the meaning of the word "person" or other general words in statutes dealing with capacity for holding office or position -I do not know that we have had it in connection with voting. There has arisen quite recently in the province of Quebec the case of Langstaff vs. the Bar of the province. This court of first instance rejected the claim of the lady to be admitted to the Bar, and the Court of Appeals confirmed that judgment. I have before me only the report of the Superior Court, and it does not give the exact text. The reporter, when he comes to the place where the judge read a section of the Act, simply indicates the section read, and does not give the wording, and I have not the statute before me. I am not clear that the question is as to the word "person." But in effect the claim was that a candidate complying with certain things would be entitled to be admitted to the Bar, and, though the candidate was spoken of as "he," yet under the interpretation which they have there as we have it here, the masculine form of expression included the feminine, unless incompatible with the context, and that because no exception was made excluding women, a woman was entitled to become a member of the profession. The Court of Appeals held, in accordance with the principles which I have been trying to make clear, that women were not included and that a woman was not entitled to become a member of the profession. This is an addition to the English case which has- been cited. I am also aware of a case in the province of New Brunswick, in which as I recollect it an endeavour was made by a lady to compel the Bar of the province to admit her to the
profession, but her application met the same fate as that of her sister in Quebec.
I have not had the advantage of reading the case, but I am told that the question was dealt with very fully and in a very conclusive manner by Chief Justice Barker of that province.
So, I think one may safely say that, in the present condition of the law, women in all the provinces stand upon the same footing, and that women in none of the provinces are entitled to vote in a Dominion election. While I think one may safely say that, I do not wish to appear dogmatic or to suggest that what I have said is the last word on the subject and that the subject is not open to discussion. But I have been asked to give my opinion, and I am very happy to give it for what it is worth.
I have little doubt, if any, that what I have just said, namely, that women in all the provinces stand on the same footing, and that in none of the provinces are women entitled to vote in a Dominion election, is sound. At all events, this can be said with a very great degree of certainty, that woman's claim to the right to vote in Dominion elections, no matter in what province she may reside, is very far from being sure under the present state of the legislation. I should imagine that any one who desires that women should be given the right to vote would realize that the only way in which that can safely be brought about would be, not the way suggested by the hon. member, but by direct aotion of this Parliament.
As I said, I do not desire to intervene in the debate on the question whether or not the vote should be given to women. The question, to my mind, is so many-sided, and calls for the consideration of such numerous, varied and important matters, and it is one whose decision is fraught with such very grave consequences, that I certainly would not attempt to speak upon it without much more careful preparation than I have had in this case-for I had not contemplated taking part in this debate. On that question, then, I abstain from taking part in the discussion. I have given what I believe there is to be said in favour of my view on this other question, in the hope that, whether I am absolutely right or not, I may at all events have served the good purpose of giving to hon. members some useful information bearing on it.

No one could find fault, I am sure, with the views expressed by the learned and hon. Minister

of Justice (Mr. Doherty). Whether we agree with his conclusions or whether we dissent, the argument he has presented is certainly one well worthy of consideration.
The motion of the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) has been supported, altogether on the statement and assumption that woman is the equal of man, and that she is entitled to all the rights and privileges given to man under our constitution. No one at this date will dispute such a statement; it is accepted everywhere, I believe, if not in all its consequences, at least in its principle, as beyond doubt or controversy. Everybody admits that woman is the equal in intelligence of man. Yet, my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) will admit that this is a proposition of very recent growth. The Minister of Justice has just presented to the House a very learned argument to show that at common law the position of woman was not the position of man, and she could not claim the privileges which have been, ever since the origin of the British Constitution, the privileges and the rights of the male sex. In fact, it is only within a very recent period, not anterior to the last days of the eighteenth century, that the declaration was heard in the civilized world that in no way was woman the inferior of man.
I think the man who, in the last century, brought the matter more forcibly to the attention of the civilized world than any person else was John Stuart Mill. Other writers before him had taken the same .position, but he it was who brought it to a climax by promoting a very active and very important agitation in Great Britain in favour of extending to women the same rights, particularly in -Tegard to voting, as were extended to men. The agitation has been of long duration; everybody knows that the idea has been of very slow growth and that in England it is only within the last year or so that the principle has been at last conceded that women ought to have the same privileges as men in regard to the franchise. As has been stated by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), the recognition of the fact that women should have the same rights as men was made subject in England to a qualification by which women are still placed in a position of inferiority in that a man can become a voter at twenty-one years of age, but a woman must reach the age of thirty years before she can exercise that right.

In the outlying parts of the British Empire the idea has made much more rapid advance; in fact, in Australia and in New Zealand for many years past women have exercised the right to vote and as far as my information goes the system has worked satisfactorily. In our own country the idea has also progressed, but it has progressed on geographical lines, so to speak. In the West the idea is universally accepted. In British Columbia, in Alberta, in Saskatchewan, in Manitoba, in Ontario, in all of these provinces, women are to-day granted the same privilege as the male sex with regard to voting. East of the province of Ontario the idea has made no progress whatever. In Quebec, while women have the right of voting in municipal deletions under certain.'conditions, in so Jar as provincial and Dominion elections are concerned, the idea has never been entertained or even agitated. The same condition, I think, prevails in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. In Nova Scotia, while the idea has been agitated, by a recent vote of the legislature, the privilege has been denied to women. It is only within the last six or seven weeks that a resolution was introduced into the legislature of Nova Scotia to give to women the same rights as men in political matters and the motion was voted down.
Now, the question arises, to which I shall come in a moment, whether or not the privilege having been given to women in five of the provinces of the Dominion, women have the right to take part in Dominion elections as well as they have to take part in provincial elections. But whilst I shall come in a moment to the argument which has been presented by my hon. friend. I would say that the debate is not confined to the proposition whether or not women in the provinces in which the franchise has been granted, that is to say British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario, have a right to vote in Dominion elections, but the question goes much farther. The resolution is to the effect that the privilege of voting should be given to the women in every province of the Dominion. This is the resolution of my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland):
That, in the opinion of this House, the question of extending the franchise to women should engage the attention of the Government at the present Session.
I would observe immediately that whilst everybody, would agree that it would be

right, in view of the argument of my hon. friend from South Oxford, that women should be given the same privilege as men, they should not be given more privileges than men. The idea which would prevail if this resolution should pass would be that this Parliament would give to women the right to the franchise when Parliament has refused to give the same right to men because it has 'accepted the franchise in regard to men from the provinces.
This debate presents to our consideration the question as to the body which, under our constitution, should be given the privilege of regulating the franchise. Should it be the Dominion Parliament or the local legislature? It goes without saying that every legislative body should have the right to determine the franchise under which it is elected. Every legislature has that right, as an historic right, unless it is deprived of it by the letter of the constitution itself. I would call the attention of the House to the fact that the United States Congress has no authority at all over its own franchise, and that it cannot legislate as to who shall be the electors to choose the members of Congress. That right is relegated to the state legislatures. Here is the American constitution:-
All legislative powers herein granted shall he vested in a Congress of the United States, which shall consist of a Senate and House of Representatives.
Section 2:
The House of Representatives shall be composed of members chosen every second year by the people of the several States, and the electors in each State shall have the qualifications requisite for the electors of the most numerous branch of the State Legislature.
I would like the House to remember that the great legislative body of the United States, one of the most powerful legislative bodies on the face of the earth, has no control whatever over its own electors and must take them as they are provided by every state. There may be a different franchise in each of the forty-five states of the Union. In some they have woman suffrage, in others they have not; in some they may have a wide franchise and in others a restricted franchise, but the fathers of the American Constitution were of the opinion that after all the body best suited to determine the qualification of voters was the local state legislature. Under our own Constitution it is very different. Our own Constitution gives us absolute power in this Parliament to determine what shall be the franchise under which the members of this House shall be elected. Section 41 of the British North America Aht says:-
Until the Parliament of Canada otherwise provides, all laws in force in the several provinces at the Union relative to the following Matters or any of them, namely:

the Qualifications and Disqualifications of Persons to be elected or to sit or vote as Members of the House of Assembly or Legislative Assembly in the several Provinces, the Voters at Elections of such Members, the Oaths to be taken by 'Voters, the Returning Officers, their Powers and Duties, the Proceedings at Elections, the Periods during which Elections may be continued, the Trial of Controverted Elections, and Proceedings incident thereto, the vacating of Seats of Members, and the Execution of new Writs in case of Seats vacated otherwise than by Dissolution,-shall respectively apply to Elections of Members, to serve in the House of Commons for the same several Provinces.
Nothing is clearer 'than that language. Until the Parliament otherwise provided, all the laws of the provinces with regard to franchise, not only those which existed at that time, in 1867, but those which might be enacted from time to time, we were to form the franchise which would apply in every province for the elections of members to this House. These laws were to constitute the provincial franchise, and were alsp to be the franchise on which, in any of these provinces members of this House were to be elected. This provision remained in force until 1885. The members of this House, from the 1st of July, 1867 until the session of 1885, were elected under the provincial franchise, such as it was in every province. In 1885 this Dominion Parliament passed a Dominion Franchise Act and constituted a franchise of its own for the election of members of this Hpuse. This law remained in force until 1898. In 1898 it was repealed. I may say-and I do not know whether or not this will meet with the approval of hon. members opposite, although I think they will agree-that to a large part of the population the Act of 1885 was not satisfactory. It was not found to work harmoniously. In 1898 it was repealed, and we returned to the provincial franchise, and I am not aware that there has been since then any objection to the franchise. From 1898 up to this date the franchise for the election of members of this House has been the franchise of each province, as it might be enacted from time to time. Everybody is aware that the local franchises were not like the laws of the Modes and Persians, they were frequently amended. Let me recall an amendment with which the members from the province of Ontario are very familiar. At one time, when we had the property qualification for voters, before we had, as we have now in almost all the provinces, universal manhood suffrage, an important amendment was passed in On-

tario to give the sons of farmers the right to vote. It so happened that, in many a household, the farmer had one or two sons, grown up men, working with him on his farm, who had not the franchise. The law very properly gave it to them, and they qualified on the real estate of their father.
I listened with interest to the speech of the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland). It was on a very broad scale and a very high plane, and I have no fault to find with the sentiments he uttered. But I would ask my hon. friend and every member of this House to agree with me that the place to regulate the franchise, bearing in mind the provision of the British North America Act that this Parliament can exercise powers for the peace, order and good government of this country, is not in this House but in the local legislature. The franchise is a right which can not be granted upon a universal scale. Our peace, order and good government depend largely upon the local conditions in each community. There are communities in which woman franchise can be exercised properly and others in which it could not. Let me take one or two cases. In France, for instance, where assuredly women have reached a very high mental level, just as high as in any other country, there has never been any demand from any body of men or any large body of women to have the franchise granted to women; while on the other side of the channel, in England, there has been an agitation which has lasted for years and which has sometimes taken a very acute form, sometimes has gone very far, to a dangerous extent even, to have women given the franchise. Why is that? It is a matter of education; and by education I do not mean simply the intellectual development of the mind, I mean social conditions, domestic conditions, and all those things which lead a class of the community in a certain direction. In England, where representative institutions have been in force for centuries, women to-day and for a long time past, at least since the middle of the last century, have taken a very active interest in political matters. In France women have not taken the same part, and so while you have on the two sides of the channel two of the most civilized nations of Europe, on one side there is the desire, which has taken a very acute form, to have the franchise given to women, and on the other side, in France, the ques-

tion has never become a matter of serious discussion, although some ladies have attempted to bring it up.
Another consideration which goes to show that the franchise is largely a matter of education is this.: I shall contrast what has taken place in Ontario not later than a few months ago, during the last session, when women were granted the franchise, and what has taken place in some states of the American Union. After all, we are very close to the United States. Their conditions are very much our own, their people are of the same birth and blood and of the same education as we are. In Ontario, where the franchise was granted to women a few months ago, only a few weeks ago a motion was made to make women eligible for membership in the legislature, and the very same legislators, the very same men who five minutes before had given the franchise to women, refused to make them eligible for membership. I do not say that was wrong, but it is the case. On the other hand, in the Congress of ithe United States there is a lady who is a member of Congress from the state of Montana. I believe that in several states of the Union women are eligible, as well as being electors. In Ontario they consented to make them electors, but would not make them eligible. What argument do I take from this? The argument I take from this is that the franchise and all the consequences of the franchise are largely matters of education, of local conditions, of local sentiment, and that it is therefore better to have these matters determined by the local legislatures than by this Dominion Parliament. May I give another example to which I alluded a moment ago? I referred to the province of Nova Scotia, as 'bright and intelligent a community as there is on this continent- everybody will agree in that. The province of Nova Scotia would not do what was done in the province of Ontario. Just about the time that the province of Ontario voted to give the franchise to women, the province of Nova Scotia voted not to give it. I would ask my hon. friend from South Oxford if under such circumstances, he would think it would be conducive to the peace, order and good government of this country that we should force on the province of Nova Scotia woman suffrage when that province has declined to grant it for local purposes?
Did the legislature vote on that matter, or was it submitted to the people?

It was the
legislature, I understand.
The ladies themselves had no say in the matter?

No, they did not have any spy 'in the matter, 'because the local legislature refused them the right. After all, these matters have to be decided by the legislature. While I admit the broad principle that the franchise is a provincial matter, I go further and say that in every province where the legislature has given to women the right to vote in provincial elections, they should be allowed to vote in Dominion elections also. The hon. Minister of Justice presented a very able argument to show that while in the provinces of Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia the women have the Tight to vote in provincial elections, they have not the right to vote in Dominion elections. As the hon. member for St. John city has stated, though the women in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta have the right to vote in provincial elections, they have not .the right to vote in Dominion elections. With all respect to the Minister of Justice, may I present this view:	in my humble judgment the contention which he has made is too narrow and of too technical a construction. My hon. friend, basing his opinion upon very learned authorities, argues that at common law women had not the right of suffrage, and that when in 1898 we reverted to the franchise adopted by the respective provinces, we could not have contemplated that in the future women might have that franchise. The answer to that is to be found in two sections of the Act which are reproduced in chapter 6 of the Revised Statutes, and which define the qualifications of voters in Dominion elections. I quote section 10:
The qualifications necessary to entitle any person to vote at a Dominion election in any province shall, except as herein otherwise provided, be those established by the laws of that province as necessary to entitle such person to vote in the same part of the province at a provincial election.
My hon. friend argues that at that time Parliament could not have contemplated the extension of the franchise to women. I say that Parliament did contemplate that, because in section 32 of the same Act these words appear:
In the Provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, except as in this Act otherwise provided, every male person shall he qualified to vote.	:	1
In the first section which I read, it is stated that every person, other than persons who are excepted, shall have the right to vote. If in any one province, only persons who are males have the Tight to vote for members of this Parliament I would say that in every other province, only persons who are males should have a like right. That would seem to me to be a reasonable conclusion, it makes our franchise to this Parliament uniform in that respect.
The Minister of Justice stated with much candor that he has not given to the matter all the thought which he would have given to it if he had expected to take part in this debate. There is another view, therefore, which I should like to present. In 1898, exercising our supreme and sovereign power to define the nature of the franchise to be exercised in Dominion elections, we determined to accept the provincial franchise. We decided that the franchise under which every member of the House of Commons should be elected should be the .franchise of the province from which he came. If he comes from the province of Ontario, the franchise shall be that of the province of Ontario; if from the province of Quebec, the franchise under which he is elected shall be the franchise of that province. I submit, not as a violent legal supposition, but as a matter of common sense, that, having chosen to accept the franchise created by the respective provinces, we decided to take the franchise not merely as it existed then, but as it might exist at any time in the future. If therefore the franchise of any province is different to-day from what it was in 1898, under the legislation then enacted, we take the franchise as it is to-day, and we have said that we shall accept it as it exists to-morrow, next year, or at any time. It seems to me that this is a reasonable interpretation of the statute. It may or may not he a legal interpretation. I was a lawyer in my day, and I know that it is rather presumptuous to interpret the law, because the law should be interpreted by the courts. But if my hon. friend has any doubt on this point, the peace, order and good government of Canada require that we should make it clear that in all the provinces which have given the franchise to women in respect of provincial elections, the franchise should be given to women for Dominion elections as well. I would not go beyond that. I do not care, for instance, to give the franchise to the women of my own province. I belong to a gallant race, which, I think, always takes a fair view in matters pertaining to the female

sex, but I do not w-ant to give the franchise to the women of my own province, because they do not seem to desire it. Bui in Alberta, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, Ontario, we should give the franchise to women in respect of elections to the House of Commons. As to Saskatchewan and Alberta, the franchise has been granted to women in respect of Dominion elections.
In this debate, and also on a previous occasion, when the matter was discussed, I heard the opinion expressed that we should have in Canada a double electorate, one for the Dominion House of Commons, which would decide national issues, so to speak, and ianother to dispose of local matters. In my estimation, nothing would be more detrimental to the unity of our country. We have already too many divisions, and it would be most inadvisable to create another. Moreover, the constitution does not contemplate anything of the kind. The constitution contemplates that there should be a Dominion Legislature, and provincial legislatures representing the same electoral body. In one legislature certain classes of questions are to be determined ; in the other domestic questions are to be determined; but it is not one electorate to deal with certain questions and another electorate to deal with other questions; it is the same electorate to dispose of the different classes of questions, one class being assigned to one legislature and the other being assigned to the other legislature, and it is in this view that I think we must persevere. Up to the present I believe nothing but the 'best effect can result from having the same electorate determine all questions, great or small, which come before it. I would for my part depreciate it extremely if we were to say to one class of the people of this country: You are good enough; we can make you British subjects, but we will not give you the privilege of British subjects. In my judgment nothing could be more detrimental to the future of Canada than that. I throw out this suggestion en passant. I hope the question will not come before the House; but on the present occasion, it is sufficient to suggest that if there be any doubt at all, the law should be, amended so as to put it beyond doubt that in all the provinces of the Dominion in which women have the franchise in provincial matters, they should have the right to exercise the franchise not only in provincial matters but in Dominion matters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may deal for a few moments with some of the contentions which my right hon. friend has advanced, I will then proceed to the general question which was discussed at some length by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley). My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in his opening remarks, said that whether or not women should have the same right as men, they certainly should not have greater rights. I do not quite understand the significance of that remark, because if the franchise should be extended to women in all the provinces of Canada, they would not be exercising any greater rights than the men; they would be exercising precisely the same rights by having a voice in the selection of members of this House. My right hon. friend also alluded to the fact that the constitution of the United ' States is different from our own in this respect: that this Parliament has complete and absolute power in the determination of the electorate which shall select its members, whereas in the case of the United States Congress the electorate is determined by the law of each State. I do not know whether my Tight hon. friend intended to suggest by that that although our constitution gives to this Parliament greater powers in that respect than that enjoyed by Congress, we should nevertheless follow the principle embodied in the constitution of the United States rather than that embodied in our own constitution. If my right hon. friend intended to suggest that, I for one would not be inclined to agree with him. He also alluded to the fact that in the British North America Act there is to be found a provision which says that, until the Parliament of Canada otherwise legislates, the qualifications of electors shall be those which were in force in the several provinces at the time of Confederation as amended from time to time by the provincial legislatures. Provisions of a similar nature with regard to other subjects are to toe found in the British North America Act; provisions of a similar nature are to be found in the Constitutional Acts of Saskatchewan and Alberta. The purpose of those provisions is perfectly obvious; it was to prevent any hiatus during the period which must intervene before the newly-created legislature could exercise its functions. That and nothing more, so far as I understand, was the purpose of those provisions. .

In' answer to the Minister of Justice my right hon. friend took the ground that sections 10 and 32 of the Dominion Elections Act make it perfectly clear that the view put forward by my hon. friend 9 p.m. from St. John is the correct view and that the opinion given by the Minister of Justice is inaccurate for the reasons stated. My right hon. friend said somewhat definitely and distinctly that women were clearly in contemplation when the Dominion Elections Act was passed, and he cited those two sections which I will take the liberty of reading again. Section 10 says:
The qualifications necessary to entitle any person to vote at a Dominion election in any province shall, except as herein otherwise provided, be those established by the laws of that province as necessary to entitle such person to vote in the same part of the province at a provincial election.
When my right hon. friend bases an argument upon that, he begs the question, because the question raised by the Minister of Justice was as to the meaning of the word "person." [DOT] If the argument of the Minister of Justice is correct in that respect, then the view put forward by my right hon. friend falls to the ground, because it comes back to the meaning of the word "person" as used in the Statute; and when he bases upon section 10 the view that qualifications are to he established by the province in respect of women as well as men and that the qualifications so established shall be binding upon this Parliament until it otherwise legislates, he leaves entirely out of view the fact that all that argument depends upon the meaning which you are to give to the word "person" as used in that section.
Then he alludes also to section 32, and he founds an argument upon the fact that in that section the expression "every male person" is used. It can hardly have, been within the contemplation of Parliament, when this legislation was passed, that women should be entitled to vote in one part of the country and should not be entitled to vote in another part. It seems to me that the argument which my right hon. friend conceives do be in his favour is entirely against him, because it is abundantly evident from this statute that no such distinction as that which my right hon. friend seeks to draw was ever intended. The use of the words "every male person" in section 32 strengthens rather than weakens the argument of the Minister of Justice with regard to the word "'person." It cannot have been in contemplation
by the Parliament of Canada in enacting this legislation that if provincial legislation in Ontario or British Columbia should grant the franchise to women, they should become entitled to vote at federal elections, whereas, if the provincial legislatures of Saskatchewan and A-lberta should do the same thing, the women there should not be entitled to the franchise, in both cases it being presumed that no further legislation had been enacted by this Parliament. I venture to think that the argument advanced by my right hon. friend in that regard is not an argument in his favour, but is an argument in favour of the view put forward by the Minister of Justice.
My right hon. friend seems to be under the impression, as the hon. member for St. John also seemed to be, that we have adopted absolutely the qualifications established in the several provinces of Canada. I would like to point out that we have done nothing of the kind. We have accepted their qualifications for the time being, and in accepting those qualifications, we have been acting under the provisions of the British North America Act. We have simply taken for the time being the qualifications established by the provincial legislatures, but we have not taken them in their entirety, because section 11 makes this provision:
No person possessed of the qualifications generally required by the provincial law to entitle him to vote at a provincial election shall be disqualified from voting at a Dominion election merely by reason of any provision of the provincial law disqualifying him from having his name on the list or from voting,-
(a)	the holder of any office; or,
(b)	any person employed in any capacity in the public service of Canada or of the province; or,
(c)	any person belonging to or engaged in any profession, calling, employment or occupation ; or,
(d)	any one belonging to any other class of persons who, although possessed of the qualification generally required by the provincial law, are, by such law, declared to be disqualified by reason of belonging to such class.
My right hon. friend says tbat this ought to be a matter for local consideration and determination in every instance. The legislation which he brought down in this Parliament and which was enacted lays down a different principle altogether. It declares that notwithstanding the determination of a provincial legislature, certain persons shall have the right to vote although the provincial legislature declares they shall not enjoy that right. This Parliament, in dealing with the question, looked at it from a broad federal standpoint, and not from a

provincial standpoint alone. It accepted the qualifications established by provincial legislatures with certain exceptions, which I have just read, and as to those exceptions it said that the will of this Parliament should prevail and not the will of the provincial legislature.
But I do not stop there. I have dealt with a portion of this enactment, which says that certain disqualifications which may from time to time be enacted by a provincial legislature shall not prevail so far as the right to vote for members of this House is concerned. I can turn to another section and show, as was pointed out this afternoon by the Minister of Justice, that certain persons whose names may appear on the provincial list shall nevertheless not be qualified to vote at elections of members of this House. I allude to Section 67, which declares :
67. The following persons shall be disqualified and incompetent to vote at any election:-
(a)	the judges of every court whose appointment rests with the Governor in Council;
(b)	Persons disfranchised for corrupt practices under this Act;
(c)	Persons disfranchised under the Disfranchising Act;
(d)	Any person who at the time of an election is a prisoner in a gaol or prison undergoing punishment for a criminal offence, or is a patient in a lunatic asylum, or Is maintained in whole or in part as an inmate receiving charitable support or care in a municipal poor house or house of industry, or is an inmate receiving charitable support in any institution receiving aid from the government of the province under any statute in that behalf.
Then follows a provision disqualifying any person who hires a horse, cab, or other conveyance to carry voters to the polls. So that even in the legislation alluded to the provincial enactments have not -been followed precisely. Certain exceptions have been 'made by which persons disqualified under provincial enactments are permitted to vote at elections of members of this House. There are also certain disqualifications which prevent persons whose names appear on provincial lists from voting at a Dominion election.
To come more particularly to the general question, my hon. friend the member for St. John has paid a very glowing tribute to the women of Canada for all that they have contributed to the national effort in this war, and I am sure that all of us will agree with the very eloquent expression of appreciation which fell from his lips. He followed that up by saying that this service to the state made it abundantly clear that the women of Canada were entitled to a voice in the government of the country. But after making those

eloquent references he followed with the somewhat lame and impotent conclusion that we should not give them the franchise for this Parliament unless their province had given them the franchise for provincial purposes. Now, if the principle which my hon. friend laid down is a good one, it seems to me that by no means does it lead to the conclusion at which he ultimately arrived, and I was very greatly surprised that a gentleman of his great legal acumen and thorjughly logical mind should have followed up such a premise with such a conclusion. So far as that is concerned, if the franchise should be granted to the women of Canada, I would not put forward the view that it is to be given to them as a reward for service. Their service has been given from the heart, from a sense of duty, from devotion to their country and to the cause which it represents. They gave that service with no idea of seeking any such reward as this, or any reward 'at all; they gave it from a ser se of duty. I would put forward their claim to a voice in the government of this country because in the great national emergency which confronts us at this time, and which involves not only the effort of the men fighting at the front, but the whole national effort of the country from men and women alike, they have showed themselves worthy to take a part in the government of this country, and they have thereby made abundantly clear what I believe was clear before, their right to a voice lin the government of the country in which they live.
My hon. friend from St. John has alluded to the experience of other countries. We have 'the experience of other countries, of Australia and New Zealand, for instance. The right hon. gentleman himself stated that the result of granting the franchise to the women of Australia and New Zealand had, as he believed, been satisfactory; I myself have never heard anything to the contrary. He took the point that this is more or less a matter of local concern, a matter on which public opinion is slowly being educated, and he seemed to apprehend grave consequences from the granting of the franchise to women in those portions of our country where the question of their right has not been greatly agitated. I do not appreciate the force of that view. My right hon. friend spoke of the peace, order and good government of Canada. What disorder, what injurious results are to be apprehended from giving to the women of Canada the right to exercise their franchise? It does not appear to me that there is any grave danger of public disorder if we should

give to the women of every province of Canada the right to vote in federal ejections. I know that a great many reasons, more than I would venture to recall to-night, have been put forward against any such proposal. The inability of women to bear arms in defence of their country, the supposed loosening of family ties, the view that it is the head of the family who should represent it, the danger of emotional legislation-all these and many other considerations have been put forward against the view that women should.be given the vote. But for my part, I do not think that any serious danger is to be appr ehended on any such score. If we should deny the right to vote to all those incapable of bearing arms in defence of the country, we should cut out a great many men, even men of military age. But no one would pretend for a moment that any snch principle as that should be followed. And so I think, with regard to all these considerations I have mentioned and which come to my attention at the moment, they might safely be disregarded. More than that, in the English-speaking countries and communities of this Empire, which enjoy democratic institutions, I believe there is an irresistible tendency to give to the womanhood of the Empire the Tight to have an adequate voice in government, and I believe that that tendency will act with increasing force until all the women of the Empire shall have the right to vote in the selection of those who are to represent them in the Parliaments of the nation and the Empire.
In this country we have a very peculiar position. The Parliament of Canada has seen fit, in the exercise of its complete and absolute power over this subject, to say that for the time being the qualifications which are established in the various provinces shall govern in Dominion elections. Five provinces of Canada have given the franchise to women in provincial elections. I shall not go further into the question as to whether women have the right for that reason to vote in Federal elections, because that has been dealt with by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doheity) whose view on that point must be accepted by the Government.
The question then comes before this Parliament as to what is to be the situation in the future. Are we, as suggested by hon. gentlemen on the other side, to make any necessary legislative provision that the women of those provinces, but not in any other province of Canada, shall be entitled to vote at Federal elections, or shall we
say that in dealing with questions of this character we ought to act upon some principle, land not commit ourselves blindly to follow what may be the popular opinion in any particular province at any particular time? I do not know how far my hon. friends opposite who have spoken would go in that direction. If Manitoba or British Columbia should repeal the enactment granting the franchise to women, should this Parliament immediately follow suit and deprive them of the right to vote in Federal elections?
No danger of their ever going back.
