I took the ground very deliberately, and I repeat it now, that if the provincial lists were to be accepted in all other provinces of Canada there was no reason why they should be disregarded in Manitoba and the northern part of Ontario. I do not think any good reason was ever advanced by my right hon. friend for taking that course, and eventually, after a very protracted fight, he withdrew his proposal so far as Manitoba was concerned, and accepted certain modifications, so far as northern Ontario was concerned.
I entirely agree that this question of enfranchising women is one that ought to engage the serious attention of Parliament. I am not going to commit myself with regal'd to the necessity or desirability of a Dominion franchise. I hope no such act may be necessary. I do not say that it may not become necessary. I have not brought forward any measure since we have been in power, to interfere with the Act of 1908; we are content to leave matters as they are. But I do think that the question now under debate is a very important one, and. one that ought to engage the attention of Parliament before any appeal is made to the country. I entirely agree with that, but I am not quite satisfied with the terms of the resolution which my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) has proposed. His resolution is in these words:
That, in the opinion of this House, the question of extending the franchise to women should engage the attention of the Government at the present session.
All questions as to the electorate which shall elect the members of this House are peculiarly questions for Parliament itself. The legislation in such matters is generally, and naturally, introduced by the Government of the day but it is a question in which Parliament itself is primarily concerned. I would therefore suggest the following amendment which will be an amendment t-o the original motion, if the amending motion proposed by my hon. friend from St. John should be declared out of order, or, if it is declared to be in order, it will be an amendment to his amendment:

That all the words after the word "that" in the proposed motion he omitted to the end thereof and the following substituted therefor:
In the opinion of this House the question of extending the franchise to women should engage the attention of Parliament before an appeal to the people is made.
I do not think there can be any question as to the propriety of that resolution whether the view which has been put forward by my hon. friends on the other side of the House, or the view which has been put forward by this side of the House, should be accepted. In either case it is abundantly clear that the subject should engage the attention of Parliament and I think it should engage the attention of Parliament so that the legislation which Parliament in its wisdom may see fit to enact should go into force before any general election is held. J therefore leave the matter at that with this motion which I propose either in amendment to the original motion or in amendment to that proposed by my hon. friend from St. John depending upon the decision that you may give, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, no question has more engaged the attention of Parliaments than that affecting the franchise. In England parliamentary history is filled with reminiscences, if I may use that word, of debates on the franchise in by-gone days. Whether it be the famous observation of "dishing the Whigs" by extending the franchise in one Reform Bill, or the declaration of Disraeli of that principle of household franchise which he thought would settle the whole matter, or the last Bill introduced toy Har-court for one man one vote, the franchise has always been a subject matter of much controversy and discussion. Nor has this country escaped that controversy and discussion. But it does seem to me that there are certain fundamental principles, notwithstanding what has been said here this evening, that well may guide us, that may well toe kept in sight in determining how we shall decide who are to have the right to vote on national questions, or for members who. shall sit in this House. There are certain fundamental matters, that have been, settled by statute history in this country. The first is that, when this Confederation came into existence, it was necessary to provide some franchise whereby members could be elected to this Parliament, and naturally, as in other matters, it was necessary to take the established franchise lists of the provinces that comprised Confederation. That was period number one. The second period in point of history was that period that commenced in 1885 and terminated in 1898, a period comprising some thirteen years. That was the time when we had in force a Dominion Franchise Act passed by this Parliament. During that time it was written upon the statute books that the Parliament of Canada would itself determine what should 'be the qualification of the electors who sent members to it. That was a Dominion franchise Act. That was an Act whereby, for national purposes, it was determined that certain men should have the qualification of electors for Parlia-

ment. The third period in our history commenced in 1898, and extends up to the present time. In that period the franchise of the provinces was adopted, but the provinces did not make the franchise whereby members were elected to this Parliament. This Parliament determined what the qualifications of an elector should be, but foT the purposes of determining those qualifications it was enacted that the various qualifications in force in the provinces should obtain with relation to the election of members to this Parliament. But, unfortunately, another period intervened between 1898 and 1917. That was the period during which hon. gentlemen opposite, for reasons that seemed good and sufficient to them, introduced, in 1907, and threw into this Parliament for discussion a Bill whereby it was declared that with respect to two portions of this Dominion the principle that they had laid down in 1898 should no longer obtain and that a new principle should be introduced and followed. That Bill did not pass; it was withdrawn, except with relation to the unorganized portions of Ontario. But it is valuable to look back upon that history of 1907, because it establishes a principle for which I contend, namely, the recognition on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite of the absolute right- not only the right, but the duty-of Parliament to determine the qualifications of electors who should send representatives to this Parliament. Therefore upon that point we -are on common ground. The Liberal party of 1907 enunciated a principle similar in terms to the principle enunciated by Sir John A. Macdonald in 1885, namely, that for the purposes of selecting members to represent them in the House of Commons the qualifications of electors should be determined in the Parliament in which they sat. That principle, therefore, seems to be comipon ground. Speaking for myself only, I desire to say that I have never for a single moment changed my view	since I	have been old
enough to think logically o-n the subject, and that view is that this Parliament should fix and determine the* qualifications of those who elect members to this body.
I said the other evening and I desire to repeat it, that it is -perfectly clear that for the purpose of selecting members to a municipal council or to a provincial legislature, it is competent for and the duty of the municipal council or the provincia1 legislature to fix the qualifications of its 964
electors. Under the British North America Act, section 92, defining the powers of the provinces, the provinces are charged with responsibility with respect to matters of local interest. It is no concern of the province to deal with those matters of national import upon which must always rest the destiny and future of this nation. But with respect to the federal powers, it is only necessary to -turn to section 91 of the British North America Act, where we find that this Parliament is charged with responsibility for the peace, order and good government of Canada, not in respect to one province or to another province, but in respect to all the provinces, whether it be British Columbia in the west or Nova Scotia -in the east. Its legislation should be of universal application and aimed at the supreme purpose of providing for the peace, order and good government of the commonwealth. That being so, it is necessary. that we should legislate for the defence of the realm, for the safety and liberty of our citizens, for the defence of their property and their rights. These are national matters, for the life of a citizen in British Colnmhia is just, as important as the life of a citizen in New Brunswick, and property, in the broad sense of that term as used in section 91 of the British North America Act, must be the subject matter of preservation by the state just as -much in the central prairie provinces as in the provinces by the sea. So that our duty is national; our obligations are Dominionwide. That being so, I submit, Mr. Speaker, as I did the other evening, that we should lay -down a principle and, in the words of Disraeli, let that principle work to the end, being confident that, having declared for	the principle,	in	its application it	will work no hardship to
individuals, however much it may effect this class or that. And in seeking for a principle upon which to determine national franchise-not a provincial or a local franchise; not a municipal franchise, but a national franchise-which will effect the well-being of the State as a whole and of its citizens as a whole, I ventured the other evening to lay down a principle, which, I submit, is founded upon the common history of mankind, running through the text-books and through all literature upon the subject since civilization began to emerge from barbarism, namely, that nationals should determine national issues; that nationals should determine national exist-

ence; that nationals should fix and determine national destiny. I will not to-night repeat the classes of men whom I believed were nationals: men who were British subjects, and naturalized citizens under certain limitations. Whatever may have been the view of individuals in this House before 1914, we at least now know, having regard to the history of the United States, to the history of some parts of our own country, and to the trend of events overseas and on this continent, that there are men who have taken the oath of allegiance either in the United States or to our own Sovereign, in whom the ties of blood and nationality are so strong that in the midst of a great conflict in which the existence of the fatherland whence they came may be at stake and who, for reasons that to them seem good, but to us seemed bad, show no sympathy for and give no support to our ambitions either as a State or in connection with the war that we are carrying on. They have seen fit to indicate, sometimes clandestinely and sometimes openly, a preference for the well-being of the land from whence they came rather than a desire to support by their conduct and their purse the campaign that is being carried on by the land of their adoption. No man who reads the history of the United States during the last three years or, for that matter, who will read with me the history of my own country as I have seen it during the last three years will, for a single moment, question the fact that naturalization alone is not sufficient to constitute a man a national in the sense in which that term is used.
I went further, because I pointed out-and now I have the opportunity to elaborate it-that when the Privy Council had to deal, in the Japanese case, with that point, they laid down this doctrine, that the exercise of the franchise is not a right, but a privilege conferred by the State that grants it, and far from being a right, it as a privilege of such importance that too great care cannot be exercised in its grant. Therefore, the legislation of the province of British Columbia that denied the right to the Japanese to be placed upon the register, notwithstanding the fact that he was a British subject, was upheld by the Privy Council, because, in the words of the court delivering judgment, it was felt that the legislature of the province of British Columbia must be at all times the best judge as to what would be for the interest of that province. In the same way this Parliament, speaking in the same terms for Can-

ada as a whole, must ever be the best judge as to what is for the benefit of Canada as a whole, and not for any portion of Canada that is now called a province.
If the principle, then, for which I contend-and I submit there is a principle-be declared, then it follows that no provincial legislature can declare that principle. That principle can be declared only by this sovereign Parliament, and as that is the case, and as it is essential that a principle should be of universal application, it follows that the mere adoption by this Parliament of the ever changing franchises, of nine provinces can never be regarded as an application of a principle that is sound from a national standpoint. My hon. friend from Bed Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) the other evening spoke of manhood franchise, believing apparently that there was such a thing throughout Canada as a franchise law universal in its character. That is not the case; there are in Canada as many franchises for the election of members to this Parliament as there are provinces. That is unsound, because it represents no principle, and unless there be a principle of universal application there should be no law based upon it. Therefore, I say: Why should a gentleman representing a constituency in the province of British Columbia be sent here by an electorate differently composed from the electorate of a constituency in the province of Pirince Edward llsland which sends a representative here? That is the neat 'question. Should a gentleman who represents, in this Parliament, a. constituency in Ontario be chosen by an electorate registered upon a register upon different qualifications from those of an electorate in a constituency in Quebec which also has the right to chopse a representative? Should one who comes from the province of Alberta or Saskatchewan represent a body of electors chosen by qualifications for national purposes different from the qualifications of a body of electors in Nova .Scotia who also send representatives to Parliament? That is the neat problem. What makes for the peace, order and good government of Canada as a whole? It is the laying down of a principle of universal application with reference to the selection of members of Parliament. And I contend that a gentleman who represents in this Parliament iany federal constituency does not represent an inferior or a superior body of men merely because he happens to be chosen from a province where in the one case there is manhood franchise, and in the other, restricted franchise.

Wliat have we had in the province in which I have lived for many years? In the province of Alberta since 1905 and in the province of Saskatchewan since 1905 we have had a franchise made 'by whp-m? by the legislatures of Albeirtia and Saskatchewan? No, by this Parliament, and once the franchise is made by this Parliament, in fulfilment of its rights under its constitution to legislate for the peace, order and good government of Canada as a whole, I say:	Why should npt the principle that
governs with respect to Alberta and Saskatchewan, whereby in those provinces- this Parliament fixes the terms and
10 p.m. conditions under which a man shall exercise his franchise for federal purposes, he extended to every part of this Dominion? That is the principle for which I contend. It cannpt, I believe, be successfully contended for a single moment by any hon. member that a principle shall have application in Alberta and .Saskatchewan and at the same time find no operation in Manitoba or British 'Columbia. That, I submit, cannot 'be so, and if this Parliament was sound in the exercise of its undoubted jurisdiction in legislating as to who should vote for members to be elected in those two provinces, it is doubly true that at this moment when the great issues of life and death and the future existence of this country are at stake, it should legislate fully; it should legislate with a principle; it should legislate having regard to the conditions under which we live and in such a way as will ensure the continued existence in this Canada of ours of British institutions. That is the principle which I lay down and for which I contend. It is for that reason I submit, that this Parliament should deal with matters of federal franchise and not leave it in the way in which it is now.

That being so, I should think much evil should fall on the head of my hon. friend because he- evidently

thought evil of civil servants voting under a Conservative Government and thought well of them voting after his friends came into power in 1896. In any case the facts are that in Nova Scotia there was a statute that precluded civil servants of a certain class from voting in provincial elections, hut after the advent to poweT of the Liberal party in 1896, my learned and honourable friend introduced into the legislature a Bill whereby he repealed that section, there being a Liberal Government in power at Ottawa. Then what ha/ppened? In 1898 a Dominion Franchise Act was passed by this Parliament, and it specially provided that the men who could not vote in Nova Scotia because they were civil servants should be able to vote for Dominion purpo-ses.
Mr. MoKENZIE:	It was repealed long
before 1906.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton):
speechtext: I had not intended to say anything upon this question, but having heard the learned and eloquent address of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) I think some explanation is called for from mysellf as to the way in which I understand some of the principles to which he has referred. I do not think he is going to carry out in practice the broad principles which he chooses to lay down to-night. He said early in his speech that every representative body should have the full say as to the qualifications of those who shall elect its members. On that principle every municipal council must have the right to create the franchise under which its members shall be voted for, and the same is true of every school board. I do not think the principle laid down by the hon. gentleman could be carried out successfully. I think the hon. gentleman forgets that the same voters are represented in the municipal council, the local legislature, and this Parliament. It is the same conscience, the same intellect, the same power in each case. That being so, why should not the man who is qualified to vote for members of the municipal council or for members of the legislature be qualified to vote for members of this House as well? Why should there be separate enactments in these cases? For the last twenty years the present Franchise Act has worked successfully from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and no one has any quarrel with it so far as I know. I would ask the hon. member for Calgary whom would he suggest as proper parties to be left off the list? Would he suggest the man who has no property of his own? Would he suggest the man who lives with his parents and who has no separate property upon which to qualify? Will anybody stand up in this House and say that there is any person left off the list by their province who should be .put on, or put on who should be left off?

Yes, all those who own a dual allegiance .and are under mili-
^
tary obligations to an enemy state should be left off.
That is a state of things that is not known in this country, so far as I am aware.
Are not .there aliens fighting for Canada in the trenches who owe a double allegiance?
They have lost that by reason of their fighting. That is the point I made the other evening.

to take the place of the home. These are the only questions that appeal to me. As to what has been discussed by the Minister of Justice and the hon. member for St. John I do not wish to offer any opinion.

Mr. Speaker, I shall only occupy a very few minutes of the time of the House. As to the legal arguments that we heard this afternoon from the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), if he had anything clear in his mind, or if he was able to make anything clear to the other legal lights in this House, he certainly was not able to make anything clear to the ordinary layman because when the hon. member was through it seemed to me that the matter was more muddled up than it was when he started. However, not being a member of the legal profession myself, I am probably not competent to pass judgment on a matter of that kind. The few remarks that I have to make will be altogether aside from the legal end of the argument. In the province from which I come women have been given the vote for the legislature. That was the first province in the Dominion to grant the right of voting to women. The women, and the men too, in Saskatchewan are very anxious that the women should be given a vote for members of the Dominion House. That can be accomplished, as I understand the matter, only by an amendment to the Dominion Elections Act that is in force so far as the elections in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta are concerned. By a very sligh amendment, women can be given the vote in those provinces. But it does not seem to me that it is the intention of the Prime Minister to give women a vote at the present time. This is the resolution that we are discussing; proposed by Mr. Sutherland, the member for South Oxford.
That, in the opinion of this House, the question of extending the franchise to women should engage the attention of the Government at the present session.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) moves an amendment t-o this motion exactly in the siame words until you come down to the words " the present session," and my right hon. friend then suggests that it should read " prior to an appeal to the country." Nobody in this House, or in this country, knows any better than my right hon. friend that the term of this Parliament ends on the 7th day of October next, within six months; so that if my right hon. friend wants or intends to give votes to the women, either of the prov-

inces that have given the local franchise to women or to the women of all Canada, he must take action -at this session; if he is going to accomplish anything action should be taken now. But my right hon. friend seems to be taking a very quiet, smooth way of doing the women of Canada out of a vote for the next Dominion election. That is how his attitude looks to me; I cannot take any other view of it. If that is not a correct view, perhaps my right hon. friend or somebody else on that side of the House will explain.
Just a word as to what the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) said about restricting the franchise. I should like to ask him what he would do in the case of an alien, a man from -an enemy country, Austria, Germany, or Turkey, who came to Canada years ago, settled here, became a British subject and brought out his young sons with him. These sons have since grown up and have, perhaps, gone to the front to defend Canada and now lie buried in France and Flanders. Is my hon. friend from Calgary going to take the franchise from that British subject, the father of those boys who have sacrificed their lives to maintain the British Empire and to maintain Canada? Why, the matter is too absurd to be considered. We have heard interminable talk about cultivating a strong national sentiment. Are you going to cultivate a strong national sentiment in Canada by disfranchising the fathers of men who have gone to the front to fight for you? Is that going to build up a British sentiment? To my mind it is absolutely absurd.
Then the 'hon. member for Calgary talks about an educational qualification. He should have consulted the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers). My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works had a hand in applying lan educational test in Manitoba when he was a minister in that province; but he repealed that legislation very shortly after he had put it into force. If my right hon. friend the Prime Minister should adopt the same course he would 'be compelled, if he should he in power to do - it, to repeal the legislation before it went very far. That is not the way to cultivate a good British sentiment, and no one knows it better than the Ministet of Public Works, because they had to repeal their Act in the province of Manitoba. It certainly looks to me, and I am sorry to have to say it, as if my right hon. friend the Prime Minister is taking a very smooth way of getting out of giving votes to the women.

Mr. Speaker, I hope I shall follow the example

of my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) and not detain the House very long at this late period. I intervene, however, to say that this debate has been a genuine surprise to myself. I have been engaged' in some capacity or other in helping in' extensions of the franchise all my life; and I was engaged in that process of enfranchisement under the name of Liberal. So, you can understand my surprise when I find in a debate like this a party *which tis called ithe Conservative party standing for a general measure of enfranchisement all over the Dominion of Canada; and a party which is called Liberal, apparently rather anxious to restrict this extension of the franchise. It simply shows that it is possible foir men to betray the qualities with which the names of the parties to which they belong have usually been associated in history. Take my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) who has just spoken. I never heard a better old-fashioned Tory speech in my life than he has just given. Why, he isays, we have had this franchise for twenty years, how can you improve it? Well, that was just the kind of argument that was put up in Great Britain against every proposed extension of the franchise Itheire, the old fashioned Tories of Great Britain always said that-[DOT]

I must say that my hon. friend misunderstood me. I was referring to the method of preparing the lists, or getting the names on the lists, not to the question of who should go on the lists; and if my hon. friend understood me as saying that I did not wish to extend the franchise any further, I must say that he did not understand what I meant. I was referring to the machinery by which the lists were prepared.

I must protest. I think I understood my hon. friend well enough. He may not like my description of him, but he said that something that was good for twenty years was good enough for now, and I challenge that statement- he does not deny that.
He does deny it. He said the machinery for preparing the lists was good enough for twenty years, and if my hon. friend wishes to misunderstand that, he can do sto.

My lun. friend gets up and repeats what I said, and says if I misunderstood wdiat he said I can do so. I leave it at that. I thought he was betraying a Conservative frame of mind, because almost in the next sentence he went on to jibe the Prime Minister because he did not hold the same view to-day as he held twenty years ago. That was another betrayal of a Conservative frame of mind. We have seen changes in the views of public men in England. Mr. Asquith was a determined opponent of woman suffrage until a few years ago. The stolid and strong Englishman that he is, he did not give way to intimidation and violence of the worst kind. But other things have arisen in the history of the world. This war has revealed a new side of the question to him, and he has changed his views. I do not know that I have any brief to defend the Prime Minister in this way, because there is no real inconsistency in arguing that so long as this is a provincial matter it should be done by the provinces. But when you are dealing wdth an anomaly created by an extension of the franchise in certain provinces which has not been made in others, you are brought up against the question of whether or not you will have a general franchise all over the Dominion. I have not the slightest hesitation in supporting views which I have enunciated previously in this House, which are in accordance with the views expressed toy the hon. member for Calgary and which are in accordance with the opinions of the vast majority of the people of Western Canada: that this is an anomaly which cannpt be allowed to continue ; that it should be put right, and that the only way of putting it right is by giving the franchise to women all over the Dominion. My hon. friend from North Cape Breton is a good-natured debater; he enlivens our proceedings with most interesting anecdotes from time to time, and I am sure that he will not mind my reviewing the remarks that he has made and arguing with him, if I may do so-for no Scotchman resents an argument, I am sure.
It must be an argument, though.

Well, I have met Scotchmen who thought that nobody could argue but themselves. That, of course, is a peculiarity of the race. In regard to the general subject, I have not the least hesitation in supporting the view that the franchise should be extended all over the Dominion. The hon. member fox North Cape Breton differed from the hon. member for Calgary as to the power of a legislative body to arrange the franchise under

which members should be elected to that body, I understood my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition to take exactly the same ground. I understood him to concede that in his opening remarks; I think that if Hansard is consulted it will be found that he took exactly the same position. But whether he did or not, I must say that I agree on the subject with the hon. member for Calgary, and not with my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) near me. I do not think that the argument with which the hon. member for North Cape Breton supported his view is a sound argument. He said that the law under which a municipality elects its members is not made by the municipality. But a municipality is not, properly speaking, a legislative body; it is largely an administrative body. I do not think, therefore, that it is on all-fours with a provincial legislature or with this Parliament. So that the position is unmistakably sound and unshake-able that a legislative body has the power to make the franchise under which its members are elected. It has been conceded -and I do not think that this view, which was stated in very clear and lucid terms by the member for Welland (Mr. German), has been differed from by anybody in the House-that women are the equals of men in intelligence and in every other quality by which we test the right of an individual to vote. If we take those two positions- that a legislative body is the proper body to constitute the franchise under which its memhers are elected, and that women are the equals of men in intelligence and in all other qualities which go to make a good citizen-then there remains no further argument on the subject. The franchise for the Dominion should be created by this legislature, and it can be very well extended to all human beings, irrespective of sex, who have arrived at that age at which they can exercise the franchise rationally and sensibly.
I listened to the speech of my right hon. leader without the slightest wish to differ from it, but it did not carry my mind in its logic. I could not follow the arguments; they were not convincing _},o me. He contended that it would be wrong-I think he almost went that far-that it would be unfair or improper to force a franchise upon the women of Nova Scotia which had been turned down by the legislature of that province. I do not think, Sir, that that is a sound argument. It is notorious that many men who have been given the fran-

chise under a general extension do not care to exercise that franchise. That is so notorious that a large section of the population of all countries in which these matters are dealt with are in favour of compulsory voting at elections. We have no sympathy with that view, but where would be the hardship of conferring upon the women of Nova Scotia the right to vote? They would be in exactly the same position as the men who have that right now, but who do not care to exercise it. I dp not see anything in that argument. The view is shared, as I understand, by the hon. member for North Cape Breton. They did not always in Nova Scotia-I have had my own 'troubles with them from time to time-my Liberal friends in Nova Scotia did not always grumble at things offered to them from other parts of the Dominion. I remember an occasion upon which they were provincial in another matter than that of the franchise-extremely provincial. And their Scotch characteristics came out especially on that occasion, because when it was a matter of steel bounties they were like Oliver Twist; they always took them and were always looking for more. Well, this Parliament, thinking that that was a very unjust method of dealing with the financial and fiscal affairs of the country, thought fit to stop that kind of gift. But the gift of another bounty in the shape of a vote for the women of the province should not, I think, be resented.
A Nova Scotia Finance Minister stopped the bounties.

Some of my hon. friends are so provincial that they never get away from their own province; he was a Dominion Finance Minister who came from Nova Scotia. I am sure that a little more study of this question and a little broadening out of views in the matter will bring all Liberals, anyway, to support the views which have been so well expressed by the right hon. Prime Minister and by the member for Calgary. I said at the beginning that this debate had been a surprise to me. Perhaps the greatest surprise about it is not the one that I expressed to begin with, but the one that I have just given a hint of-that I am in absolute agreement with the speech of the member for Calgary. I should not, perhaps, put it so strongly. We have had many differences, but so far as the main portion of his speech, anyhow, was concerned-the votes for

women-I am in absolute agreement with him, and I think he made to this House an admirable argument on that question.

Mr. Speaker, I wish
to address myself for a few moments to the amendment m.oved by the right hon. leader of the Government. I have been very much surprised at the amendment that he has moved. It is difficult to understand the reason which animated the Prime Minister in moving it. One is naturally led to *wonder what is behind the amendment, because ordinarily the Prime Minister would not move an amendment to a resolution presented by a supporter of the Government unless there was very good reason for doing so. The resolution says:
That, in the opinion of this House, the question of extending the franchise to women should engage the attention of the Government at the present session.
My right hon. friend proposes to strike out the whole of my resolution and substitute for it the following:-
In the opinion of this House the question of extending the franchise to women should engage the attention of Parliament before an appeal to the people is made.
Now, just what wias deep down in the mind of my right hon. friend when he moved , that amendment I am unable to understand. Does he mean that it is not the duty of the Gotermnent to deal with this question, but that it is the duty of some private member to deal with it? And is it the view of my right hon. friend that if some private member does not deal with it the responsibility is removed from the members of the Government and they \yill say: Oh, it was open to Parliament to deal with the subject; it was the duty of a private member to bring it up just as much as it was the duty of the Government, and no private member introduced a Bill. It seems to me it is the duty of the Government to deal with this very important question. The Dominion Elections Act is an Act over which the Government naturally has charge; it is an Act .which involves public expenditure. The Dominion elections necessarily involve a charge upon the public treasury, and, therefore the Dominion Elections Act is a statute with which the Government ought to deal and the making of amendments to that Act is peculiarly entrusted to the Government. Therefore, I apprehend that it is primarily the duty of the Government to take this matter into consideration and to . submit to Parliament a Bill providing for amendments.
For some reason or other, my right hon. friend, in his amendment, has said that the question of extending the franchise to women should engage the attention of Parliament-not at the present session, as has been proposed by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland)

but at some time before an appeal is made to the people. As one who wants to see the franchise extended, either to the women of those five provinces in which their names are placed upon the provincial lists, or to all the women of Canada, I am not prepared, as one member of this House, to allow the matter to be disposed of in this way.
What difference can it make to the hon. gentleman if before an election the matter is submitted to Parliament; the franchise will be extended to women at the earliest possible moment.

The difference is this, that, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) the life of Parliament will expire in October next. In the ordinary course of events, there can be no further session of Parliament after the present one, and therefore if we are in earnest in regard to the matter, we should say that this change should be made at the present session of Parliament. Who knows that there will be any other session? Who will suggest that there will be any other session?
Does the hon. member assert that there will be no other -session?

I can assert that this
Parliament has no power to hold another session after October of this year. I can assert that this Government has no power to call this Parliament together for another session. This Parliament absolutely will die by lapse of time in October next.
Is my hon. friend speaking for his leader?

I am speaking for myself and, as my hon. friend knows well what the law of Parliament is, no one knows better than does my hon. friend that the life of this Parliament will expire in October next and this Parliament has under the British North America Act no power to prolong its life. What may be done by another body, I do not know; but is the right of the women of this country to receive the franchise to depend upon whether or not another body may extend the life of this Parliament? Is the right of the women of this country

to have justice done to them to depend upon this question? If we are all in favour of extending the franchise to women-and we seem all to be, because there has been no expression of dissent from either side of the House-the only question is as to whether the extension should be to the women whose names are placed upon the provincial voters' lists, or whether there should be a broad Dominion measure extending the franchise to all women whether they have the right to vote for members of the provincial legislature or not. Why not let this House express the view-why should it not express the view that this measure should be brought down at the present session? It will not take long to prepare a Bill; it will not take long to put it
11 p.m. through. It apparently will not be controversial, if controversial at all in its character. Then why has the resolution been altered by the declaration that this change should be made, not during the present session of Parliament, but before an appeal to the people ' is made? I would almost think that my right hon. friend drew up that amendment through an oversight. In order, however, to put the matter beyond any doubt, I would move as an amendment to the amendment :
That there be added to the amendment the words "and it is therefore desirable that a measure having: this object in view should be submitted to Parliament by the Government during- the present session."

Does the hon. gentleman mean toy what he has said that this Parliament in this session has no power to extend the life of Parliament for another
year?
I mean that this Parliament has no power to extend its life. That power does not rest with this Parliament nor with this Government.

The	hon. gentleman
would say that this Parliament had no right last year?

It had no power last
year.

agreed to the extension last year.

This Parliament was
extended last year by the Imperial Par-ia-ment.

Can not that be done
again this year by a similar process? Will the hon. gentleman give me an answer?
[Mr. Pugsley.j

If my hon. friend desires an answer, I would say that the question ae to whether it can be properly done from time to time and under the circumstances which exist to-day, is one which requires most careful and earnest consideration.
Mr. Speaker, do I understand that the amendment to the amendment is in ordeT?
I rise to a point of order, namely, that the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. John differs in no way from the original motion and is consequently out of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: As I have just at this moment seen the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. John, I do not think I should give an opinion offhand. There is nothing to prevent the hon. member for Vancouver proceeding with his Temarks, apd I will deal later with the point of order raised by the hon. -member for St. Antoine.
Mr. Speaker, my point of order was in effect that the subamendment was only another way of moving the previous question, as it would put us back where we were before.

My hon. friend is in error. I presume he has not read the resolution carefully. The resolution says that in the opinion of this House the question of extending .the franchise to women should engage the attention of the Government at the present session. The amendment proposes that the question of extending the franchise to women should be considered by Parliament,' as Parliament is the only body that can deal effectively with it. My amendment to the amendment is that legislation should be introduced to Parliament by the Government at the present session. Neither the amendment nor the sub-amendment are at all in effect like the original' resolution.

I feel I should be remiss in my duty as representing the constituency of Chateauguay if I did not give my views on this question, particularly as I have received several communications from women's organizations in my county with respect to the subject now under discussion. We have heard it said in 1a good many quarters that women do not desire the franchise. The hon. member for North Cape Breton intimated in his remarks that the women of his province did not desire it. Be that as it may, the women of the county of Chateauguay do desire the franchise, and as the representative of that constituency I feel that it is my duty to give expression to their views and also to my own. There are a great many women's organizations throughout this country, and perhaps the most prominent is the Women's Christian Temperance Union, which for the last 30 or 40 years has been quietly working for the advancement of humanity. Some of the communications to which I refer came direct to me from the officials of a branch of that organization. If there is any organization in Canada that should be recognized I think it is the Women's Christian Temperance Union, and if they desire the vote they should have it. There are other women's organizations in this country which are doing great work to-day, the Red Cross, for instance, which was fostered and has
been nurtured by women. I feel that the women of this country who are working for the advancement of the country should be recognized by this Parliament, and I trust that the resolution as amended will be passed and become law before this Government goes out of office.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Between the motion submitted by the hon. member for South Oxford, and the amendment submitted by the right hon. the Prime Minister, and the amendment to the amendment submitted by the hon. member for St. John, we seem to be moving in a circle. The question whether the amendment to the amendment is in order is rather a delicate one to determine on such short notice, and in deference to the hon. member for St. John, -and I think it is also due the House- if it should meet with the approval of hon. gentlemen I would suggest that the debate be adjourned so that I may have opportunity to look into the matter, before giving a decision.
I have no objection to that, providing an opportunity will be given for resuming the debate.'

We will resume it at some other time.
